questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the incidence of breech presentation in singleton deliveries at term? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3%

Breech presentation refers to a longitudinal lie in which the fetal buttocks or lower extremities present first.

Incidence: Approximately 3% of singleton pregnancies at term

Breech presentation is more common earlier in pregnancy, but most fetuses spontaneously convert to cephalic presentation before term.

Types of breech presentation:

• Frank breech → hips flexed, knees extended (most common)
• Complete breech → hips and knees flexed
• Footling breech → one or both feet presenting

Risk factors:

• Prematurity
• Multiple pregnancy
• Placenta previa
• Uterine anomalies
• Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 50-year-old female patient presents with a 4*3cm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, which is not fixed to the skin or the chest wall. A lymph node of 2cm is palpated in the right axilla. No mass is palpated in the opposite breast. Which of the following investigations would you perform on this patient?

1. Bilateral mammography
2. PET Scan
3. Biopsy of the breast mass
4. USG guided biopsy of the lymph node
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 & 4

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of breast malignancy with locoregional spread with unlikely distant metastasis.  For further evaluation of this lesion, bilateral mammography, a biopsy of the breast mass and a USG-guided biopsy of the suspicious lymph node need to be performed in order to determine staging and decide on further management.

Statement 2: PET Scan is usually performed in advanced cases of breast cancer. It is not routinely used in the assessment of locoregional disease.

Statement 1: Diagnostic mammography is used to evaluate women with abnormal findings such as a breast mass or nipple discharge. Mammography is more accurate than clinical examination for the detection of early breast cancers. Mammographic features suggestive of breast cancer include a solid mass with or without stellate features, microcalcifications, irregular soft tissue shadow, spiculations and duct distortion.

Statement 3: Pathological diagnosis of carcinoma is made by a core needle biopsy (tru-cut biopsy) or fine-needle aspiration before any type of treatment is started.

Statement 4: The presence or absence of axillary lymph node involvement in breast cancer is one of the most important prognostic factors for determining staging and treatment. Ultrasound-guided lymph node biopsy should be done in patients with suspicious or clinically palpable lymph nodes.

Ultrasound features suggestive of breast cancer include a hypoechoic, irregular mass with indistinct, angulated or spiculated margins, acoustic shadowing, ductal extension and a branched pattern of mass.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Cardiac edema and neuropathy are seen in which of the following vitamin deficiencies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

Cardiac edema and neuropathy are associated with the deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1).

Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy, irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and proprioception. As the disease progresses, increased intracranial pressure, meningismus, and coma develop.

Wet beriberi (cardiac) is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, and edema. It is commonly seen in the refugee camps where people consume polished rice based monotonous diets. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability.

Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy.
questions.learning: Thiamine Cardiac edema and neuropathy are associated with the deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1). Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy, irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and proprioception.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Seman's squeeze technique is used for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Premature ejaculation

Seman's squeeze technique is used for premature ejaculation, to prolong the time period until ejaculation.

Seman's technique (stop-start technique): It is a variation of the squeeze technique where a man approaches the point close to ejaculation and then stops before ejaculation and relaxes before starting stimulation again. This method prolongs the time until ejaculation by relying on behavior modification.

Other treatments for premature ejaculation:

• Squeeze technique (Master and Johnson's technique)- as a man approaches a climax, he squeezes the tip of the penis just below the head of the penis. The pressure is held there until the sensation of impending orgasm diminishes. The process can then be started over again so that over time a man prolongs the time period until he reaches ejaculation.
• Sensate focusing- refocussing on the non-coital aspects of sexual activity.
• Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)- delays ejaculation. e.g.- dapoxetine, paroxetine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The graph depicting the post-mortem cooling process is typically expected to have what shape?
questions.explanation: The graph representing the post-mortem cooling process (algor mortis) characteristically follows a Sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This curve is composed of three distinct phases. Initially, there is a "temperature plateau" or "post-mortem lag" period where the body temperature remains nearly constant for 1–3 hours as internal heat production briefly continues and heat loss is slow. This is followed by a rapid, linear drop in temperature as the body cools toward the ambient environment. Finally, as the body temperature approaches the room temperature, the rate of cooling slows down again, creating the flattened tail of the "S". A Linear (Option C), Hyperbolic (Option A), or Parabolic (Option D) shape would not accurately represent these distinct physiological phases. Understanding the sigmoidal nature of algor mortis is essential for forensic pathologists when estimating the Time Since Death (TSD). Various environmental factors, such as clothing, body habitus, and humidity, can significantly influence the slope and duration of this cooling curve
questions.learning: The graph representing the post-mortem cooling process (algor mortis) characteristically follows a Sigmoid (S-shaped) curve. This curve is composed of three distinct phases.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Countercurrent mechanism is present in which of the following parts of the body?

1. Eye
2. Testes
3. Kidney
4. Gut
5. Lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2,3,4,5 are correct

The countercurrent mechanism is present in the testis, kidney, gut, and lungs.  When the inflow runs parallel to, counter to, and in close proximity to the outflow for some distance it is called as the counter current mechanism.

Spermatogenesis requires a temperature considerably lower than that of the interior of the body. The testes are kept cool by heat exchange in a countercurrent manner between the spermatic arteries and veins.

The concentration of the urine by the kidney requires an osmolality gradient. This gradient is produced by the loop of Henle as counter-current multipliers and maintained by vasa recta as counter-current exchangers.
The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:

1. The high permeability of the thin descending limb to water ( via aquaporin-1)
2. Active transport of Na+ and Cl- from the thick ascending limb, thereby diluting the tubular fluid.
3. The inflow of tubular fluid from proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule.

The countercurrent mechanism is used in the villi to decrease the oxygen availability for local metabolic reactions of the gut. Hence this will increase the blood flow in the intestine during gastrointestinal activity.

Countercurrent exchange of oxygen is seen in the lungs as well.
questions.learning: 2,3,4,5 are correct The countercurrent mechanism is present in the testis, kidney, gut, and lungs. When the inflow runs parallel to, counter to, and in close proximity to the outflow for some distance it is called as the counter current mechanism.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Positron emission tomography is based on which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose metabolism

Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism.

PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron.

A glucose analog called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is used. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and thus accumulates within the cell. The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.

Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.
questions.learning: Glucose metabolism Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism. PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to the hospital with features of severe malnutrition and marked dehydration, requiring prompt intravenous fluid therapy. To ensure effective rehydration and correction of electrolyte disturbances, which intravenous fluid would be the most appropriate choice for management in this patient?
questions.explanation: For a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with significant dehydration, standard aggressive rehydration protocols must be modified to prevent heart failure and electrolyte overload. The recommended IV fluid in this specific high-risk scenario is Ringer's Lactate (RL) with 5% Dextrose. This fluid provides both volume and glucose to prevent hypoglycemia, which is common in SAM. Standard Normal Saline (Option C) or DNS (Option D) contains too much sodium, which can lead to life-threatening fluid overload in a malnourished heart. ORS (Option A) is the fluid of choice for oral rehydration but is not appropriate for the "immediate medical intervention" of IV resuscitation in a severely dehydrated patient. The IV infusion rate in Sam must be slow and meticulously monitored for signs of respiratory distress or increasing liver size, which indicate early cardiac failure
questions.learning: For a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with significant dehydration, standard aggressive rehydration protocols must be modified to prevent heart failure and electrolyte overload.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child with mental retardation, blindness, and muscle weakness was investigated and was found to be deficient for Hexosaminidase-A enzyme. She is most likely suffering from ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tay-sachs disease

Tay-Sachs disease is due to the deficiency of the enzyme Hexosaminidase A which degrades GM2 gangliosides.

Tay-Sachs disease is a rare genetic disorder characterized by the deficiency of the enzyme Hexosaminidase-A. This enzyme is responsible for breaking down a fatty substance called GM2 ganglioside, which is found primarily in nerve cells.

Without sufficient Hexosaminidase-A activity, GM2 ganglioside accumulates in the cells, particularly in the brain and nerve tissues, leading to the characteristic symptoms of Tay-Sachs disease.

Clinical features of Tay-Sachs disease are :

* Loss of motor skills

* Seizures

* Hyperacusis

* Macrocephaly

* Macular cherry-red spots

* Neurodegeneration

* Blindness

* Muscular weakness

Other options:

A. Krabbe's disease: Krabbe's disease, also known as globoid cell leukodystrophy, is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme galactosylceramidase. It leads to the accumulation of a lipid called galactocerebroside in the nervous system. The symptoms of Krabbe's disease may include muscle weakness, developmental delay, and vision problems, but mental retardation is not typically a prominent feature.

B. Fabry's disease: Fabry's disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of a fatty substance called globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in various tissues and organs. Fabry's disease can present with a wide range of symptoms, including neurological manifestations, skin abnormalities, kidney problems, and cardiovascular complications. However, mental retardation is not a typical feature of Fabry's disease.

D. Gaucher's disease: Gaucher's disease is an inherited disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of a lipid called glucocerebroside primarily in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Gaucher's disease can present with various symptoms, including hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged liver and spleen), anemia, and skeletal abnormalities. Mental retardation and blindness are not characteristic features of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 53-year-old postmenopausal woman is found to have endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hysterectomy

Among the given options, for post-menopausal women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia, the next step in management would be a hysterectomy because the risk of progression to cancer over time approximates 29 per cent.

Due to a high rate of finding concurrent invasive malignancy coexistent with atypical hyperplasia, the ideal management is to perform a fractional curettage with hysteroscopy before proceeding with a hysterectomy (with removal of both tubes and ovaries).

Endometrial hyperplasia is endometrial thickening with a proliferation of irregularly sized and shaped glands along with an increased gland-to-stroma ratio.

Classification of endometrial hyperplasia:

• Simple hyperplasia is characterised by dilated or cystic glands with round to slightly irregular shapes, an increased glandular-to-stromal ratio without glandular crowding, and no cytologic atypia.
• Complex hyperplasia has architecturally complex (budding and infolding) crowded glands, with less intervening stroma without atypia.
• Atypical hyperplasia refers to cytologic atypia and can be categorised as simple or complex, depending on the corresponding glandular architecture. Criteria for cytologic atypia include

•

• large nuclei of variable size and shape with lost polarity
• increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios
• prominent nucleoli
• irregularly clumped chromatin with parachromatin clearing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of colchicine in the acute treatment of gout?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of chemotaxis

Colchicine relieves an acute gout attack by inhibiting microtubule polymerization through binding to tubulin, thereby preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, phagocytosis, and degranulation. This suppresses the inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals without affecting serum uric acid levels.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase: Mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, which reduce uric acid production for long-term gout management.
• B. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase (COX): Mechanism of NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin, naproxen), which reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammation.
• D. Blockade of IL-1 receptors: Mechanism of anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), used in selected refractory cases of acute gout.
questions.learning: Inhibition of chemotaxis Colchicine relieves an acute gout attack by inhibiting microtubule polymerization through binding to tubulin, thereby preventing neutrophil chemotaxis, adhesion, phagocytosis, and degranulation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what age does a child attain half-height of the adult height?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 20 - 24 months

A child attains half of the adult height by 20 -24 months.

The normal length at birth is 50 cm, increasing to around 75 cm at 1 year of age. By the end of the second year, the length ranges from 85 to 90 cm.

From age 2 to around 12 years, there is a steady growth of about 6 cm per year. During pubertal growth spurts after age 12, females grow an average of 8 cm per year, while males grow around 10 cm per year.

By around 2 years of age, a normal child reaches half of their adult height (around 80-85 cm). Height doubles by age 4 and triples by age 12 compared to the birth length.

Between 18-24 months, a child experiences significant growth and development.

Physically, they improve their balance, learn to run and climb stairs, and reach about half of their adult height. Head growth slows slightly, with 85% of adult head circumference achieved by the age of 2 years.

Cognitive development includes the establishment of object permanence and problem-solving skills (e.g., using a stick to obtain a toy that is out of reach).

Emotionally, they display self-recognition and recognize when toys are broken. When toddlers see anything abnormal in their noses while gazing into a mirror for the first time, they tend to touch their own faces rather than reaching out toward the reflected image.

Linguistically, their vocabulary expands from 10-15 words to 50-100 words, and they start combining words to form simple sentences while understanding two-step commands (eg., give me the ball and then get your shoes).
questions.learning: 20 - 24 months A child attains half of the adult height by 20 -24 months. The normal length at birth is 50 cm, increasing to around 75 cm at 1 year of age.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on the tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the papillae does not have taste buds?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Filiform

Filiform papillae are most numerous and have a mechanical role, lacking taste buds and often keratinized.

Circumvallate, foliate, and fungiform papillae contain taste buds and are involved in gustation, making them clinically relevant in tongue carcinomas affecting taste.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient engages in strenuous exercise, skips a meal, and later consumes alcohol at a party. Alcohol intake inhibits which biochemical process, thereby increasing the risk of developing hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase produces an excess of NADH, significantly increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver. This high ratio shifts metabolic reactions away from glucose production by preventing the conversion of lactate to pyruvate and malate to oxaloacetate, both of which are essential substrates for gluconeogenesis. Hypoglycemia occurs because the body cannot synthesize new glucose once glycogen stores are depleted (common after exercise or fasting). Alcohol does not directly inhibit glycogenolysis (Option B), but it becomes the primary issue when glycogen is already gone. The HMP shunt (Option C) and ketone body formation (Option D) are not the primary pathways responsible for blood glucose maintenance. In fact, alcohol metabolism can actually promote ketogenesis. Therefore, the inhibition of gluconeogenesis is the specific mechanism behind alcohol-induced fasting hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Alcohol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase produces an excess of NADH, significantly increasing the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Acid Citrate Dextrose (ACD), used to store blood, preserves the RBCs for a period of 21 days. The storage period when adding phosphate alone and when adding adenine and phosphate together to ACD would respectively be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 21 days and 35 days

The storage period when adding phosphate alone to ACD would be 21 days and when adding adenine and phosphate together would be 35 days.

When adding phosphate to ACD, Citrate Phosphate Dextrose (CPD) is formed – It has a storage period of 21 days. There is no change in the shelf life as phosphate only increases the 2,3 DPG levels of the stored blood.

When adding both phosphate and adenine to ACD, Citrate Phosphate Dextrose Adenine (CPDA-1) is formed. It has a storage period of 35 days. It increases the shelf life by improving ATP synthesis of RBCs.

Using additive solutions containing saline, adenine, and glucose, with or without mannitol (SAGM) decreases RBC hemolysis, thus increasing the storage period to 42 days.
questions.learning: 21 days and 35 days The storage period when adding phosphate alone to ACD would be 21 days and when adding adenine and phosphate together would be 35 days.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological cause of this anomaly?
options: Failure of fusion of metanephric duct
questions.explanation: The anomaly shown is a unicornuate uterus, which results from the developmental failure of one paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct. Normally, the two paramesonephric ducts must fuse at the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. If one duct fails to develop or fuse properly with its counterpart, it results in a single-sided uterine cavity, often accompanied by a small rudimentary horn. Non-fusion of the mesonephric ducts (Option A) would affect male reproductive anatomy, such as the vas deferens. "Metanephric duct" (Option C) is an incorrect term, as the metanephros forms the kidneys, not the uterus. Complete agenesis (Option D), known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, would result in the total absence of the uterus and upper vagina. Therefore, the partial failure of Müllerian duct development is the correct embryological cause
questions.learning: The anomaly shown is a unicornuate uterus, which results from the developmental failure of one paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct. Normally, the two paramesonephric ducts must fuse at the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of fever and cough for the past 3-5 days. His examination findings reveal crepitations. Chest X-ray is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
options: Apical segment of Right lower lobe consolidation
Posterior segment of right lower lobe consolidation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right middle lobe consolidation

The given clinical scenario of fever, cough, and crepitations suggests features of pneumonia. The chest X-ray showing opacities with obscuration of the right cardiac border is suggestive of right middle lobe consolidation.

This loss of clear demarcation between the normal lung and its surrounding soft structures (heart, diaphragm) is called the silhouette sign. It occurs due to loss of contrast between lungs and soft tissue when the lung parenchyma is no longer filled with air. This sign may be seen in consolidation, atelectasis, or mass lesions.

In the following images:

• Left image - red line indicates the normal demarcation between the right heart border and middle lobe of the right lung
• Right image - loss of demarcation i.e, positive silhouette sign due to right middle lobe consolidation

Positive silhouette sign and corresponding anatomical site of pathology:

• Right heart border - right middle lobe or medial right lower lobe
• Left heart border - lingula segments of the left upper lobe
• Left hemidiaphragm or descending aorta - left lower lobe
• Aortic knuckle - left upper lobe (posterior segment)
• Right hemidiaphragm - right lower lobe
• Right paratracheal stripe - right upper lobe

Other options:

Apical segment of Right lower lobe consolidation: In this case, the chest X-ray would show an opacity or consolidation in the apical segment of the right lower lobe. The consolidation would be located in the lower part of the right lung, towards the apex. The right heart border, however, would remain visible, as it is not adjacent to the apical segment of the right lower lobe.

Posterior segment of right lower lobe consolidation: A chest X-ray revealing consolidation in the posterior segment of the right lower lobe would show an opacity in the lower part of the right lung, more posteriorly. This would not affect the visibility of the right heart border, as it is not adjacent to the posterior segment of the right lower lobe. In a posteroanterior (PA) chest X-ray, this consolidation may be difficult to appreciate, but it would be more evident in a lateral view.

Loculated pleural effusion: In a chest X-ray showing a loculated pleural effusion, there would be a fluid collection within the pleural space. This fluid collection would appear as a well-defined opacity, typically with a convex border facing the lung parenchyma. It may appear as a lenticular shape, conforming to the space between the lung and chest wall or diaphragm. The loculated pleural effusion would not create a silhouette sign with the right heart border, as it is located in the pleural space rather than the lung parenchyma.
questions.learning: Right middle lobe consolidation — The given clinical scenario of fever, cough, and crepitations suggests features of pneumonia. The chest X-ray showing opacities with obscuration of the right cardiac border is suggestive of right middle lobe consolidation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common side effect of orlistat?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Steatorrhea

The most common side effect of orlistat is steatorrhea.

Orlistat is an anti-obesity drug that acts by forming a covalent bond with the lipases in the gastrointestinal tract and thus decreasing fat absorption. When a usual dose of 120 mg TID is taken it blocks the digestion and absorption of dietary fat by around 30%. After discontinuation of the drug fecal content returns to normal within 48-72 hours. They can also inhibit the absorption of many fat-soluble vitamins like Vit A, D, E, and K

Side effects of orlistat:

* Steatorrhea: most common, due to the impaired absorption of dietary fat.

* Gastro-intestinal side effects: flatus, increased defecation

* Renal injury: the unabsorbed fat binds with calcium, forming renal stones that can lead to oxalate nephropathy.

* Osteoporosis: due to deficiency in Vit D and calcium

Pearl PF0170: Anti-obesity drugs

Centrally acting anti-obesity drugs: The biologic effect of these agents on appetite regulation is produced by augmentation of the neurotransmission of three monoamines, norepinephrine, serotonin (5-HT) and dopamine.

* Phentermine – Sympathomimetic (Phentermine is usually used in combination with topiramate)

* Lorcaserin – Selective 5-HT2C receptor agonist

Peripherally acting medications:

* Orlistat is a synthetic hydrogenated derivative of a naturally occurring lipase inhibitor, lipostatin, that is produced by the mold Streptomyces toxytricini.

Anti-obesity drugs in development:

* Bupropion: Dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor

* Naltrexone: Opioid receptor antagonist

Liraglutide: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist
questions.learning: Steatorrhea — The most common side effect of orlistat is steatorrhea. Orlistat is an anti-obesity drug that acts by forming a covalent bond with the lipases in the gastrointestinal tract and thus decreasing fat absorption.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in MEN 2B syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parathyroid adenoma

MEN 2B is caused by activating RET mutations and is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Mucosal neuromas of lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract are hallmark features.

Patients often show marfanoid habitus and may have intestinal ganglioneuromatosis causing megacolon.

Parathyroid adenoma is seen in MEN 2A, not MEN 2B, making it the incorrect feature.
questions.learning: Parathyroid adenoma MEN 2B is caused by activating RET mutations and is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma. Mucosal neuromas of lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract are hallmark features.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The given USG of lung shows:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sea shore sign

The given image shows the seashore sign seen in M-mode imaging of the normal lung.

M-mode is defined as the time-motion display of the ultrasound wave along a chosen ultrasound line. With M-Mode, even rapid motions can be displayed, measured, and recorded.

In the M-mode of USG, the motionless portion of the chest above the pleural line creates horizontal ‘waves', and the sliding below the pleural line creates a granular pattern, the ‘sand’. The resultant picture is one that resembles waves crashing in onto the sand and is therefore called the ‘seashore sign’ and is present in a normal lung.

Option A: Stratosphere sign or barcode sign is a finding in the M-mode seen as parallel horizontal lines above and below the pleural line. This is seen in pneumothorax.

Option C: There is no named sign called troposphere sign.

Option D: Mirror image artifact is seen when there is a highly reflective surface (eg: Diaphragm) in the path of the primary beam.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A frameshift mutation occurs due to the insertion of a new nucleotide at the 4th position of an mRNA sequence containing 900 nucleotides. What is the most likely outcome of this mutation?
options: No change in the final protein
No change due to RNA editing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complete change in protein production

A frameshift mutation occurs when nucleotides are inserted or deleted in numbers not divisible by 3, altering the reading frame of the mRNA.

In this case, insertion of a nucleotide at the 4th position (early in the sequence) causes:

• Shift in the reading frame from that point onward
• All subsequent codons are altered
• Often leads to a premature stop codon
• Produces a completely abnormal (nonfunctional) protein

Why other options are incorrect:

• No change in protein: Seen in silent mutations, not frameshift
• Partial protein production: More typical of nonsense mutation (premature stop without frame shift)
• No change due to RNA editing: RNA editing does not correct frameshift mutations
questions.learning: Complete change in protein production — A frameshift mutation occurs when nucleotides are inserted or deleted in numbers not divisible by 3, altering the reading frame of the mRNA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Neck examination reveals a thickened structure, as shown in the image below. What is this structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process, the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial, ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with cervical lymphadenopathy and is found to be retropositive. A fungal culture depicts a velvety growth with red diffusible pigment on the underside, as shown below. Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Talaromyces marneffei

The most likely causative organism based on the history and image given is Talaromyces marneffei (Penicillium marneffei).

T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis). It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. It is diagnosed by blood culture, which shows a mold with a powdery surface and characteristic red pigment that diffuses into the agar. Histopathological examination reveals yeast-like organisms with central septation.

Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.

Mild and moderate infections can be treated with itraconazole. Amphotericin B is recommended for severe infections.

Other options:

Option B - Blastomyces are thermally dimorphic fungi and cause blastomycosis. Primary infection usually affects the lungs, which can later disseminate through the blood to form multiple abscesses at sites such as skin and bone. Culture at 25–30 degrees Celsius promotes hyphal growth. Microscopic examination of stained specimens shows broad-based budding yeast cells.

Option C - Aspergillus colonies have a velvety powdery surface, of which the color varies according to the species. Aspergillus fumigatus is seen as dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black colored. Yellow-green growth is seen in the case of Aspergillus flavus. On microscopy, dichotomous branching at acute angles seen after staining is characteristic. It can cause invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients.

The image below shows Aspergillus niger colonies.

Option D - Pneumocystis jirovecii cannot be cultured. On being stained by methenamine silver, the cyst wall appears black under the microscope. Trophozoites can also be seen after staining. Clinical features include dyspnea, fever, and cough. It can cause lethal pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals. Diffuse bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates can be seen on chest radiograph.
questions.learning: Talaromyces marneffei — The most likely causative organism based on the history and image given is Talaromyces marneffei (Penicillium marneffei). T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Below is a diagram depicting the natural history of the disease. Which point marks the onset of symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point C

Point C represents a point where signs and symptoms appear.

Various points marked in the image represent the following:

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Luminescent stools are associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phosphorus

Luminescent stools are seen in acute phosphorus poisoning. The vomitus and stools will be luminous in the dark.

The stools may give rise to faint fumes, constituting the smoky stool syndrome.
questions.learning: Phosphorus Luminescent stools are seen in acute phosphorus poisoning. The vomitus and stools will be luminous in the dark.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with retrosternal chest pain radiating to the jaw along with difficulty in swallowing. A barium swallow study demonstrates characteristic abnormalities. Based on these clinical features and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of retrosternal chest pain (often mimicking cardiac pain) and dysphagia, coupled with a barium swallow showing a "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance, is diagnostic of Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES). DES is a motility disorder characterized by uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophageal smooth muscle. Infectious esophagitis (Option A) typically presents with painful swallowing (odynophagia) and white plaques or ulcers, not this radiographic pattern. Barrett’s esophagus (Option C) is a pre-malignant change in the mucosa and is often asymptomatic or associated with chronic reflux. Esophageal stricture (Option D) shows a smooth or irregular narrowing of the lumen, not multiple spastic segments. Diagnosis is definitively confirmed with esophageal manometry showing high-amplitude, non-peristaltic contractions. Treatment involves smooth muscle relaxants like nitrates or calcium channel blockers, and in refractory cases, a long myotomy
questions.learning: The combination of retrosternal chest pain (often mimicking cardiac pain) and dysphagia, coupled with a barium swallow showing a "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance, is diagnostic of Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The ECG of a pregnant lady having pre-eclampsia is shown below. Her vitals are stable. What is the best step in the management of the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV MgSO4

The given ECG showing a wide QRS complex tachycardia with waxing and waning QRS amplitude points to the diagnosis of torsades des pointes. As the patient is hemodynamically stable, intravenous MgSO4 is the treatment of choice.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) has a continually changing QRS morphology. Polymorphic VT that occurs in individuals with congenital or acquired prolongation of QT interval is referred to as torsades des pointes. Patients present with near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest.

IV MgSO4 is highly effective for both treatment and the prevention of recurrence of long QT-related ventricular ectopic beats that trigger torsades des pointes.

If magnesium alone is ineffective, isoproterenol infusion or pacing, to a rate of 100-120 depolarization/minute usually suppresses VT recurrences.

If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, then immediate defibrillation should be done.

Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation

Used in unstable PSVT, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse
Used in ventricular tachycardia without a pulse, and ventricular fibrillation.

Shock is delivered in sync with the R wave (in absolute refractory period)
Shock is delivered at any time during the cardiac cycle.

Monophasic - 100 to 200J
Monophasic - 360J

Biphasic - 50 to 100J
Biphasic - 120 to 200J

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: Tight junction is located at which part of the cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Apicolateral

Tight junctions sit like a “sealant ring” at the apicolateral border, preventing leakage between cells and maintaining polarity. Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are located at the apicolateral border of epithelial cells, forming the most apical component of the junctional complex. Two Key Functions:

1.     Barrier function → blocks paracellular transport

2.     Fence function → maintains polarity (apical vs basolateral domains)

| Junction | Location | Function | Key Proteins

| -------- | -------- | -------- | ------------

| Tight junction | Apicolateral | Barrier, polarity | Claudin, Occludin

| Adherens junction | Below tight | Cell adhesion | Cadherins

| Desmosome | Lateral | Mechanical strength | Desmoglein

| Gap junction | Lateral | Communication | Connexin

Adherens junctions and desmosomes lie more basally.

Clinical correlations:

1. Leaky gut / diarrhea

• Loss of tight junction integrity → ↑ permeability

2. Cholera toxin

• Affects ion transport → overwhelms junctional barrier

3. Blood-brain barrier

• Tight junctions are extremely well-developed

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with recently noticed scrotal swelling. On examination, the testis is palpable separately from the swelling, and the swelling transilluminates positively. The patient reports no pain or discomfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates positively, and importantly, the testis is palpable separately from the swelling. This combination of findings indicates that the swelling is extra-testicular and cystic, arising from the epididymis, rather than surrounding the testis. A spermatocele is a retention cyst of the epididymis that contains milky fluid rich in spermatozoa. It typically occurs in adult men and is most commonly located above and behind the testis. On examination, it is soft, fluctuant, non-tender, and shows positive transillumination. A key distinguishing feature is that the testis can be clearly felt separately below the swelling. Although an epididymal cyst has similar features, in clinical exams, spermatocele is the preferred answer in adults presenting with these classical findings. Hydrocele is ruled out because it surrounds the testis, making it difficult to palpate separately
questions.learning: The patient presents with a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates positively, and importantly, the testis is palpable separately from the swelling.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with epilepsy was put on retigabine TDS. Now phenytoin is being added. Which of the following changes should be made to retigabine?
options: Stop retigabine and start on carbamazepine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase the dose

The dose of retigabine should be increased when phenytoin is added because phenytoin can decrease the plasma concentration of retigabine when given together.

Retigabine is also known as ezogabine. Metabolism of the drug occurs by glucuronidation and acetylation. Its half-life is about 7-11 hours and hence requires thrice-daily dosing. When it is administered with phenytoin or carbamazepine there may be a reduction in the plasma concentration of the drug. So the dose of retigabine should be increased when given along with these drugs.

It is a potassium(K+) channel opener that enhancer transmembrane potassium currents mediated by the KNCQ family of ion channels. It was approved as an adjunctive agent for focal onset seizures of patients above 18 years. But because of its adverse effects like retinal abnormalities and blue pigmentation, the production of the drug was discontinued by the manufacturer.

Other drug interactions of phenytoin:

It is an inducer of the enzymes CYP2C8/9, CYP3A4/5, and other CYPs. It is also an inhibitor of CYP2C9/19.

• Phenobarbitone can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin. But the overall interaction is unpredictable as both the drug enhance each other's degradation by enzyme induction.
• Phenytoin and carbamazepine induce each other's metabolism.
• Valproate increases the level of unbound phenytoin by displacing the protein-bound form and decreasing its metabolism.
• Phenytoin increases the metabolism of steroids, oral contraceptives, doxycycline, theophylline, etc by enzyme induction.
• It produces competitive inhibition of warfarin metabolism. (Increased risk of bleeding when given together)
• Drugs like chloramphenicol, warfarin, isoniazid, and cimetidine can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin and cause its toxicity.
• Sucralfate decreases the absorption of phenytoin by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Increase the dose — The dose of retigabine should be increased when phenytoin is added because phenytoin can decrease the plasma concentration of retigabine when given together.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The below-given image is characteristically seen in which of the following type of leprosy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Borderline leprosy

The given image shows a case of borderline tuberculous leprosy, or dimorphous leprosy, as evidenced by the cutaneous, rash-like discoloration of the patient’s skin. This generally overlies the back, and crosses the midline. So, the best choice would be Borderline leprosy.

Microscopically, there is diffuse epithelioid cell granuloma with very scanty lymphocytes and no giant cells; the papillary zone is clear and the nerves are swollen slightly by cellular infiltrate. Acid-fast bacilli are present in moderate numbers.

The borderline leprosy patients are immunologically unstable and are at an increased risk of developing immune-mediated reactions. Type 1 lepra reactions that occur most commonly in mid-borderline leprosy patients, are delayed hypersensitivity reactions caused by increased recognition of mycobacterial leprae antigens in skin and nerve sites.
questions.learning: Borderline leprosy — The given image shows a case of borderline tuberculous leprosy, or dimorphous leprosy, as evidenced by the cutaneous, rash-like discoloration of the patient’s skin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman with a family history of Marfan syndrome presents with unilateral tonsillar swelling, and visible pulsations are noted on oral examination. What is the most likely cause of this tonsillar enlargement?
questions.explanation: Patients with Marfan’s syndrome have a genetic predisposition to connective tissue weakness, making them highly susceptible to arterial aneurysms. A unilateral tonsillar or pharyngeal swelling that exhibits "visible pulsation" is a red-flag sign for an aneurysm of the adjacent carotid artery . The internal carotid artery (ICA) passes immediately lateral to the tonsillar fossa in the parapharyngeal space. An extracranial (Option A) aneurysm in this segment can protrude medially, mimicking a tonsillar mass. Intracranial aneurysms (Options B and D) would present with neurological deficits rather than a visible oropharyngeal mass. The external carotid artery (Option C) is further removed and less likely to present as a tonsillar swelling. Biopsy or incision of such a "pulsatile mass" is strictly contraindicated due to the risk of catastrophic hemorrhage. Diagnosis must be confirmed with CT or MR angiography. Therefore, the anatomical location and Marfan association indicate an extracranial internal carotid artery aneurysm

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presented with heartburn and increased salivation. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was done, and the biopsy result is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Barrett’s esophagus

This image indicates the diagnostic features of Barrett’s esophagus.

The histological image above shows the transition between normal squamous epithelium and the mucin-filled glands, indicating intestinal-type metaplasia with plenty of goblet cells.

Barrett’s esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) characterized by intestinal metaplasia within the esophageal squamous mucosa. It is a premalignant condition that confers an increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Hence, patients diagnosed with Barrett’s Esophagus must be subjected to a regular surveillance endoscopy annually or with 2-year intervals, provided no dysplasias have been detected. The presence of dysplasia is associated with prolonged symptoms, longer segment length, increased patient age, and Caucasian race.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with central cyanosis and a radiological image of a boot-shaped heart with oligemic lung fields. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for cyanosis in the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

The image above shows a boot-shaped heart. Cyanosis, oligemic lung fields, and a boot-shaped heart (cœur en sabot in French) point towards tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

Radiological features: "Coeur en sabot" is due to cardiac apex elevation as a result of right ventricular hypertrophy. The cardiac silhouette has been likened to that of a boot (“coeur-en sabot”). The hilar areas and lung fields are relatively clear because of diminished pulmonary blood flow or the small size of the pulmonary arteries. The aorta is usually large.

Clinical findings in TOF:

* Right ventricular hypertrophy, causing a left anterior hemithorax bulge.

* Single S2 or soft P2 because of the stenotic pulmonary valve

* Systolic thrill in the left sternal border in the 3rd and 4th parasternal spaces.

* The large 'a wave in the jugular pulse is a reflection of the forceful contraction of the right atrium at the end of diastole, as there is reduced distensibility of the hypertrophic right ventricle.

* There is a loud and harsh systolic murmur due to the right ventricular outflow tract(RVOT) obstruction. It becomes louder, longer, and harsher as obstruction increases in severity from mild to moderate.

However, in severe obstruction, especially during a tet spell, the murmur becomes less prominent as the blood is shunted towards the aortic valve and not through RVOT.

Other options:

Option B: ASD is characterised by an abnormal opening in the atrial septum, allowing communication between the right and left atria. Ostium secundum ASD is the most common type of ASD.

Option C: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart defect. Commonly seen in maternal diabetes and fetal alcohol syndrome.

Option D: TGA on chest x-ray shows a classical egg on string appearance.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman develops edema, visual disturbances, and signs of heart failure after consuming a particular food item. What is the most likely adulterant responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances (specifically glaucoma), and heart failure is characteristic of Epidemic Dropsy. This condition is caused by the consumption of mustard oil adulterated with Argemone mexicana seeds, which contain the toxin Sanguinarine. Sanguinarine causes widespread capillary damage and permeability. BOAA (Option B) is the neurotoxin found in Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dal) that causes Neurolathyrism, a spastic paralysis of the legs. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (Option C) cause Veno-Occlusive Disease (VOD) of the liver, leading to ascites. Aflatoxin (Option D) is a potent carcinogen produced by fungi on stored grains and is a major risk factor for liver cancer. Epidemic dropsy is a serious public health issue in areas where adulterated cooking oil is sold. Early diagnosis and supportive care are essential, as the cardiac failure can be rapidly fatal. Testing for the presence of Argemone oil is done using the simple Nitric Acid test or chromatography

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can be given without dose modification in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
questions.explanation: Linagliptin is unique among the DPP-4 inhibitors because it is primarily excreted via the enterohepatic system (bile and feces) rather than the renal route. Consequently, it does not require any dose adjustment regardless of the severity of renal impairment or CKD. Saxagliptin (Option B), conversely, is eliminated renally and requires a reduction in dose once the glomerular filtration rate falls below a certain threshold. Repaglinide (Option C), a meglitinide, is mostly metabolized by the liver, but current guidelines still suggest cautious titration in severe renal failure. Glyburide (Option D) is a second-generation sulfonylurea that is metabolized into active metabolites excreted by the kidneys ; it is generally contraindicated in CKD due to the high risk of prolonged, severe hypoglycemia. For clinicians managing diabetes in renal patients, Linagliptin offers a significant advantage by maintaining safety and efficacy without the need for complex dosage modifications based on fluctuating creatinine levels
questions.learning: Linagliptin is unique among the DPP-4 inhibitors because it is primarily excreted via the enterohepatic system (bile and feces) rather than the renal route.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In this scenario, what is the mode of transmission by which the condition was passed from the grandmother to the father and then to the boy?
options: Autosomal recessive AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.explanation: The inheritance pattern described involves the direct transmission of a trait from a grandmother to her son (the father) and then to his son (the grandson). This vertical transmission across three generations, including male-to-male transmission, is the hallmark of Autosomal Dominant inheritance. In X-linked dominant (Option A) and X-linked recessive (Option B) patterns, a father cannot pass the trait to his son because he only contributes his Y chromosome to male offspring. Autosomal recessive inheritance (Option D) typically presents as a horizontal pattern (skipping generations) and requires both parents to be carriers, which is inconsistent with the direct lineage shown here. Therefore, because the condition is passed directly from father to son through consecutive generations, it excludes X-linked and recessive possibilities, confirming that the gene is located on an autosome and is dominant in expression
questions.learning: The inheritance pattern described involves the direct transmission of a trait from a grandmother to her son (the father) and then to his son (the grandson).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Ga-68 PSMA PET scan is used to diagnose which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) PET scanning is a specialized and highly sensitive imaging modality used specifically for the diagnosis and staging of prostate cancer. PSMA is a protein that is overexpressed on the surface of most prostate cancer cells. The Ga-68 tracer binds specifically to this protein, allowing for the detection of even very small areas of cancerous tissue. It is particularly valuable for detecting localized recurrence or metastatic disease when traditional scans like bone scans or CT are negative or inconclusive. Lung cancer (Option A), colon cancer (Option C), and liver cancer (Option D) are typically staged with other modalities, most commonly FDG-PET or contrast-enhanced CT. PSMA-PET has revolutionized the management of prostate cancer by providing more accurate staging, which guides the choice between radical surgery, radiation, or systemic therapies
questions.learning: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) PET scanning is a specialized and highly sensitive imaging modality used specifically for the diagnosis and staging of prostate cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man presents with a three-year history of persistent perianal discharge and discomfort, raising suspicion of a fistula-in-ano. Which investigation is considered the most accurate and reliable for confirming this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MRI of the pelvis is currently the gold standard and most accurate investigation for the evaluation of a fistula-in-ano. It provides exceptional detail of the pelvic floor anatomy, accurately identifies the primary track, detects secondary extensions or branch tracks, and localizes associated abscesses. This detailed mapping is crucial for surgeons to avoid recurrence and prevent injury to the anal sphincters during operative repair. A fistulogram (Option A) is often unreliable as it may fail to fill the entire track and does not visualize the internal sphincter relation. Ultrasound (USG) (Option B), particularly endoanal ultrasound, is useful but operator-dependent and less comprehensive than MRI. CECT (Option C) provides some information but lacks the soft-tissue contrast necessary to distinguish complex tracks from surrounding pelvic muscles. Given the patient's three-year history suggesting a potentially complex fistula, MRI is the most reliable imaging modality to ensure a successful surgical outcome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which class of ovarian tumor does clear cell carcinoma of the ovary belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epithelial cell tumor

Clear cell carcinoma of the ovary is a type of epithelial cell tumor.

Epithelial ovarian tumors arise from the mesoepithelial cells present on the ovarian surface. 80% of all ovarian cancers are epithelial cancers.

Clear cell carcinoma is also known as mesonephroid tumor. The histopathology of clear cell carcinoma reveals large cuboidal epithelial cells with abundant clear cytoplasm characteristically forming tubules, glands, and small cystic spaces. These cystic spaces are lined by hobnail cells. They are clear cells showing large dark nuclei protruding into the lumen. It is a highly malignant tumor.

Malignant epithelial tumors can spread widely via transcoelomic spread. It can spread through the capsule onto the peritoneal surface, omentum, intestinal viscera, and sub-diaphragmatic space. An ascitic tap will reveal blood-stained fluid with tumor cells. It may also spread to the para-aortic nodes and cause metastasis in the other ovary, liver, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Epithelial cell tumor Clear cell carcinoma of the ovary is a type of epithelial cell tumor. Epithelial ovarian tumors arise from the mesoepithelial cells present on the ovarian surface.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released from SA node in response to increase in blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetylcholine

When BP rises, the body tries to slow the heart down

An increase in blood pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, increasing vagal output to the heart. Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine at the SA node, slowing heart rate.

↑ Blood pressure

↓

Baroreceptors activated (carotid sinus, aortic arch)

↓

Signals to medulla

↓

↑ Parasympathetic (vagal) output

↓

Acetylcholine released at SA node

↓

↓ Heart rate (bradycardia)

This parasympathetic response reduces cardiac output and helps normalize blood pressure. The SA node is primarily controlled by cholinergic vagal input in this reflex.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and a sensation of fullness in the left upper abdomen for two months. Examination reveals marked splenomegaly. Laboratory findings show hemoglobin 10 g/dL, WBC count 165,000/mm³, and platelet count 300,000/mm³. The peripheral smear demonstrates metamyelocytes 15%, promyelocytes 30%, and myeloblasts 45%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of weight loss, fatigue, and massive splenomegaly, accompanied by extreme leukocytosis ( cells/cu.mm). While Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (Option B) is characterized by massive splenomegaly and a full spectrum of myeloid cells, the definitive diagnostic feature in this case is the blast count. The peripheral smear reveals a myeloblast count of 45%. According to WHO criteria, an acute leukemia diagnosis is established when the blast count in the blood or bone marrow exceeds 20%. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Option A) involves mature lymphocytes. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Option C) involves lymphoblasts and is more common in children. Although CML can present similarly, the high blast percentage (45%) signifies either de novo Acute Myeloid Leukemia or CML in blast crisis. Given the options provided, Acute Myeloid Leukemia is the most appropriate and definitive diagnosis for this high-blast presentation

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A sigmoid configuration along with tapering beak-like deformity at the lower esophageal sphincter on barium swallow is a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Achalasia cardia

Achalasia cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and absence of normal esophageal peristalsis, resulting from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.

Characteristic barium swallow findings:

• Dilated esophagus with a sigmoid (S-shaped) configuration in advanced disease.
• Smooth, tapering “bird’s beak (beak-like)” narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).
• Delayed emptying of contrast into the stomach.

Diagnostic evaluation:

• Gold standard: High-resolution esophageal manometry showing:

• Incomplete LES relaxation
• Increased LES resting pressure
• Absent peristalsis

• Upper GI endoscopy: Performed to exclude pseudoachalasia (e.g., malignancy).

Why not the other options?

• A. Diffuse esophageal spasm: Barium swallow shows corkscrew (rosary bead) esophagus.
• B. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus: Produces an irregular, shouldered narrowing, not a smooth bird’s beak appearance.
• D. Barrett’s esophagus: Diagnosed endoscopically by specialized intestinal metaplasia, not by a bird’s beak deformity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what cut-off respiratory rate will you consider “fast breathing” in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ≥40 per minute

Fast breathing (tachypnea) is an important clinical sign used in the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI/IMCI) to identify possible pneumonia. The respiratory rate cut-off varies with age. In a 2-year-old child (12–59 months), a respiratory rate of ≥40 breaths/minute is considered fast breathing.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. ≥60 per minute: Cut-off for young infants <2 months.
• B. ≥50 per minute: Cut-off for infants 2–12 months.
• D. ≥30 per minute: Below the diagnostic threshold for fast breathing in a 2-year-old.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 56-year-old female has been diagnosed with gallstones and is undergoing a preanaesthesia checkup. She has been a diabetic since the last 15 years, but sugar levels are within the limits. Which category of physical status does she fit into?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ASA II

The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative fitness and estimate perioperative risk.

ASA II — mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitations.

Quick reference for ASA-PS classification:

• ASA I — normal healthy patient
• ASA II — mild systemic disease, no functional limitation (e.g., well-controlled diabetes or hypertension, controlled asthma, current smoker, social alcohol use, obesity with BMI 30–40, mild lung disease)
• ASA III — severe systemic disease, some functional limitation (e.g., poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, diabetes with vascular complications, morbid obesity, active hepatitis, ESRD on dialysis)
• ASA IV — severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g., recent MI/CVA <3 months, ongoing cardiac ischemia, sepsis)
• ASA V — moribund, not expected to survive without surgery
• ASA VI — brain-dead patient for organ donation
questions.learning: ASA II — The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative fitness and estimate perioperative risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged man employed in sandblasting presents with hemoptysis and a productive cough, and his chest X-ray findings are suggestive of tuberculosis. Which associated condition is most likely linked to his occupational exposure?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a sandblaster presenting with respiratory symptoms and findings suggestive of tuberculosis (TB) is a classic association for "silicosis." Sandblasting involves the inhalation of fine silica dust , which causes a chronic, fibrotic lung disease. Importantly, silica is toxic to pulmonary macrophages, the primary defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Consequently, patients with silicosis have a significantly increased risk (roughly 30-fold) of developing tuberculosis, a condition sometimes called "silicotuberculosis." Asbestosis (Option A) is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer but not specifically with increased TB risk. Anthracosis (Option C) is "coal worker's pneumoconiosis" and is generally less fibrogenic than silicosis. Siderosis (Option D) is caused by iron dust and is usually a benign, non-fibrotic pneumoconiosis. The classic X-ray finding in silicosis is small, rounded opacities in the upper lobes and "eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes. Given the specific occupational history and the TB association, silicosis is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what time during the intrauterine life does talus ossification center appear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6 months

The talus bone ossification center appears in the 6th month of intrauterine life.

Nearly all secondary centers commence ossification after birth, although a few develop in the last few weeks of intrauterine life. Secondary ossification centers that are already present when an infant is born include:

* Distal femur - 7th week

* Proximal tibia - 7th week

* Humerus - 8th week

* Calcaneus - 3 to 4th month

* Talus - 6th month

* Cuboid - 9th month

Forensic medicine textbooks like Knight's Forensic Pathology (4th edition page 456), The essentials of Forensic medicine and Toxicology
Dr. K.S. Narayan Reddy (34th edition page 75) states that the talus ossification begins at 7 months instead of 6th.

The answer is as per Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice (42nd Edition page 1436)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following connective tissue degradation disorder is associated with aortic aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marfan's Syndrome

Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, leading to defective elastic fiber formation in connective tissues. Weakness of the aortic media predisposes to aortic root dilatation, aneurysm, and dissection, which is a major cause of mortality in these patients.

It is also characterized by tall stature, long limbs (arachnodactyly), lens dislocation, and skeletal abnormalities.

Why not other options:

• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Defect in collagen synthesis causing hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility; vascular complications may occur in rare types but aortic aneurysm classically associated with Marfan syndrome.
• Atherosclerosis: Causes arterial narrowing and plaque formation, not primarily a connective-tissue degradation disorder.
• Scurvy: Vitamin C deficiency causing defective collagen synthesis leading to bleeding gums and poor wound healing, not aortic aneurysm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which serotype of HPV is responsible for Ca Cervix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 16, 18, 31, 33

HPV – 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68 are associated with Ca Cervix.

Human Papilloma Virus (DNA Virus):

* The most common serotype of HPV responsible for Ca.Cervix: HPV 16

* The most malignant serotype of HPV for Ca.Cervix: HPV 18

* HPV serotype most specific for Ca. Cervix is HPV 18.

* The most common serotype of HPV associated with Squamous Cell Carcinoma is HPV 16

* The most common serotype of HPV associated with Adenocarcinoma is HPV 18

* Viral proteins required for malignant transformation are E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

* The E6 gene acts through the p53 gene, and E7 acts through the Retinoblastoma gene.

* Viral proteins required for replication are E1 and E2.

* Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or southern blot or Hybrid capture technique is used for HPV DNA detection.

As per the December 2022 WHO Position on HPV vaccines, WHO recommends the following schedule:

* A one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9-14

* A one or two-dose schedule for girls and women aged 15-20

* Two doses with a 6-month interval for women older than 21

A minimum of 2 doses and when feasible 3-doses remain necessary for those known to be immunocompromised and/or HIV-infected.

Note: Cervavac is India's first indigenously prepared quadrivalent HPV (qHPV) vaccine.

* Targeted strains: 6, 11, 16, and 18.

* Targeted group: 9-26 years of age

* Dose and route of administration: 0.5 ml, IM.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 1-year-old child is brought to the healthcare unit that you are working on. His mother mentions that he had received the first dose of DPT vaccine at 6 weeks of age but has missed vaccination since then. What would you advise the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give second dose of DPT

The advice for the patient is to give the second dose of DPT (Diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus).

DPT is a combined vaccine given for immunization against the three diseases diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus. It is given to infants as early as 6 weeks following birth. The pertussis component of the vaccine is not recommended beyond 6 years due to the decrease in the severity of pertussis infection with age. 7 years of age onwards, only Td combinations are used.

It is given in 3 doses with an interval of 4 weeks followed by booster doses at 18-24 months and at 5 years of age. The dosage is 0.5 mL and is given in the anterolateral aspect of the thigh intramuscularly. The immunization can be resumed without repeating the previous dose in case of any delayed or interrupted immunization.

Adverse effects include fever, and neurological complications such as encephalitis, convulsions, infantile spasms and Reye's syndrome.

Anaphylaxis is a contraindication for subsequent vaccination with diphtheria, pertussis, or tetanus vaccine. Encephalopathy following vaccination is a contraindication for pertussis vaccine. DT is given for successive doses.

Events such as inconsolable cry, fever more than 40.5°C, seizures with or without fever are considered as precautions, and not contraindications for DTwP.

Note: IAP guidelines state that "temperature more than >40.5°C is a precaution and not contraindication". Park's 27th Ed states that "temperature above 40°C is a contraindication to DPT". This topic is controversial, however, IAP guidelines are commonly followed by practitioners.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-week-old newborn is brought with complaints of non-bilious vomiting. On examination, a palpable mass is noted in the left epigastric region, which becomes prominent and moves during feeding. What is the most likely diagnosis in this infant?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS) characteristically presents in infants between 2 and 6 weeks of age. The hallmark symptoms include projectile, non-bilious vomiting and the presence of a palpable "olive-shaped" mass in the epigastrium, which may show movement (peristalsis) during feeding. Ultrasound is the investigation of choice, typically showing a pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm. Regarding the distractors, Esophageal atresia (Option A) presents immediately at birth with drooling and inability to feed. Duodenal atresia (Option B) presents with bilious vomiting shortly after birth and the classic "double-bubble" sign. Intussusception (Option D) usually occurs in older infants (6–18 months) and presents with a "sausage-shaped" mass and "red currant jelly" stools rather than non-bilious projectile vomiting. Therefore, the specific timing and nature of the vomiting and palpable mass definitively confirm IHPS

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following cell organelles is associated with killing bacteria and viruses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysosomes

Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and are associated with killing bacteria and viruses.

Lysosomes  are membrane-bound organelles broken off from the Golgi apparatus, containing roughly 40 different acid hydrolases (enzymes that function best in acidic pH ≤5). These hydrolases include proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases, and sulfatases.

Lysosomal enzymes provide an intracellular digestive system that digests damaged cellular structures, food particles ingested by the cells, and foreign particles like bacteria and viruses. The membrane around the lysosomes prevents the hydrolytic enzymes from being in contact with the other substances in the cell and prevents them from being digested.

When an enzyme is congenitally absent, the cell becomes engorged with the material the enzyme normally degrades. This leads to lysosomal diseases e.g Gaucher disease is caused due to a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes small bowel obstruction and paralytic ileus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colicky abdominal pain

Small bowel obstruction (SBO) is characterized by colicky (cramping) abdominal pain caused by vigorous peristaltic contractions attempting to overcome a mechanical obstruction. In contrast, paralytic ileus results from absent intestinal peristalsis and presents with diffuse, constant discomfort rather than colicky pain.

• Colicky abdominal pain is the hallmark of mechanical small bowel obstruction and helps distinguish it from paralytic ileus, in which bowel motility is absent.

Why not the other options?

• A. Abdominal distension: Seen in both SBO and paralytic ileus.
• C. Vomiting: Common in both conditions, especially in proximal SBO.
• D. Tachycardia: May occur in both due to dehydration, pain, or sepsis and is not a distinguishing feature.

| Feature | Small Bowel Obstruction | Paralytic Ileus

| ------- | ----------------------- | ---------------

| Pain | Colicky, intermittent | Constant, mild, diffuse

| Bowel sounds | High-pitched, hyperactive (“tinkling”) | Absent or markedly reduced

| Peristalsis | Increased initially | Absent

| Abdominal distension | Present | Present

| Vomiting | Common | Common

| X-ray | Multiple air-fluid levels with step-ladder pattern | Generalized gaseous distension of bowel

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient who was being treated for hypertriglyceridemia developed flushing, gout, hyperglycemia, and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nicotinamide

Niacin (nicotinic acid) causes flushing, hyperuricemia (gout), hyperglycemia, and hepatotoxicity. Correct answer is C because nicotinic acid (niacin) used for hypertriglyceridemia causes flushing (prostaglandin mediated), hyperuricemia leading to gout, hyperglycemia, and hepatotoxicity with raised liver enzymes.

Statins mainly cause myopathy and mild liver enzyme elevation. Fibrates cause myopathy and gallstones. Ezetimibe mainly reduces cholesterol absorption and is usually well tolerated.

| Drug | Key Side Effect

| ---- | ---------------

| Niacin | ⭐ Flushing + gout + hyperglycemia

| Statins | Myopathy

| Fibrates | Gallstones

| Ezetimibe | Minimal systemic side effects

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A child with loose stools for one day presented to your OPD. On examination, signs of dehydration were present and the child was given ORS. It facilitates glucose absorption through which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SGLT1

ORS facilitates glucose absorption through SGLT 1 (Sodium-dependent glucose co-transporter - 1). In a child with diarrhea, when oral rehydration solution is given, there is coupled absorption of sodium and glucose through SGLT -1.

Glucose transport may be active or passive.

Active transport of glucose takes place through Sodium dependent glucose transporter (SGLT 1 and 2). SGLT 1 helps in glucose absorption in the small intestine and renal tubules. SGLT 2 primarily facilitates glucose absorption in the renal tubules.

Passive absorption of glucose occurs through facilitated diffusion. This is carried out by Glucose transporters (GLUT) 1 -7.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident with a ruptured spleen, hypotension (BP 80/60 mm Hg), and metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely cause of his current condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with trauma (motorcycle accident), a confirmed source of massive internal bleeding (ruptured spleen), and signs of circulatory collapse including low blood pressure (80/60 mm Hg) and metabolic acidosis . This is the quintessential clinical picture of Hypovolemic Shock (specifically hemorrhagic shock) (Option C). The sudden loss of a large volume of blood results in inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia, leading to acidosis. Cardiogenic shock (Option A) results from heart failure, while Septic shock (Option B) requires time to develop from infection. Neurogenic shock (Option D) usually presents with bradycardia and warm skin following a spinal cord injury. Because the primary insult is the acute hemorrhage from the splenic rupture, hypovolemia is the definitive cause of the patient’s shock. Management mandates rapid volume resuscitation followed by urgent surgical intervention (splenectomy or repair) to stop the bleeding

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, below what heart rate are chest compressions initiated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 60

According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, chest compressions are started when heart rate is below 60/min

The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate.

* If the heart rate is less than 100/min, PPV is initially provided with bag and mask on room air, and SPO2 monitoring is done. Increasing concentration of oxygen is used to ensure adequate ventilation.

* If the heart rate is below 60, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1.

* If the heart rate still remains <60, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then IV epinephrine is given.
