questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—mouth breathing, an elongated expressionless face ("adenoid facies"), a high-arched palate, and crowded teeth—is pathognomonic for chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy . The adenoids are lymphoid tissues in the nasopharynx; when enlarged, they block the posterior choanae, forcing the child to breathe through the mouth. This chronic mouth breathing leads to the characteristic craniofacial changes described. Lingual tonsils (Option A) are at the base of the tongue and do not cause nasal obstruction. Quinsy (Option B) is a peritonsillar abscess causing acute throat pain. Tonsillar hypertrophy (Option C) involves enlarged palatine tonsils, which can cause snoring and dysphagia but are less typically associated with the "adenoid facies" skeletal changes . The provided X-ray likely shows a soft tissue mass in the nasopharynx narrowing the airway. Consequently, adenoid hypertrophy is the most accurate diagnosis for this 5-year-old child
questions.learning: The clinical presentation—mouth breathing, an elongated expressionless face ("adenoid facies"), a high-arched palate, and crowded teeth—is pathognomonic for chronic nasal obstruction due to adenoid hypertrophy .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient diagnosed to be retro-positive was started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Which of the following can be used to monitor treatment efficacy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Viral load

The viral load can be assessed in a retro-positive patient started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to monitor treatment efficacy.

HAART or combination antiretroviral therapy is the mainstay in the management of retro positive patients. It is initiated soon after diagnosis except in cases of cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis.

After initiation of therapy, a ten-fold reduction in plasma human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) RNA levels in 1-2 months can be expected. Within six months, a slower decline to <50 copies/mL is anticipated. During the first month of therapy, a rise in CD4+ T cell count is also predicted. Out of these two parameters, viral load is the better choice to monitor treatment efficacy as it is more cost-effective.

Plasma HIV RNA levels signify the rate of CD4+ T-cell destruction and the magnitude of HIV replication. It should be monitored within 2-4 weeks of initiation of therapy and after any change in the treatment regimen. It should be repeated every 4-8 weeks till the RNA levels drop to <200 copies/mL and then every 3-6 months subsequently.

The indications for change in the treatment regimen are:

• < 10-fold drop in HIV RNA levels within 4 weeks of initiation
• ≥ 3-fold increase from the nadir of plasma HIV RNA level not attributable to other causes
• Persistent decline in CD4+ T-cell counts
• Adverse effects
• Clinical deterioration

Other options:

Option C: p24 antigen is a core protein present in the capsid of the virus.

Option D: Viral serotype does not play a role in monitoring treatment efficacy. Most cases of HIV are due to HIV-1. HIV-2, another human immunodeficiency virus can also cause disease in humans.
questions.learning: Viral load — The viral load can be assessed in a retro-positive patient started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) to monitor treatment efficacy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about polyarteritis nodosa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30% is associated with Hepatitis B

One-third of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) cases are associated with Hepatitis B.

Other options:

Option A: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic vasculitis which is associated with necrotizing inflammation of small and medium-sized muscular arteries.

Option B: Patients show hypergammaglobulinemia.

Option C: PAN is rarely associated with ANCA positivity. There is no serological test for PAN. Most patients exhibit an elevated leukocyte count with a predominance of neutrophils.

PAN is usually seen in young adults, characterized by rapidly accelerating hypertension, abdominal pain, bloody stools, myalgias, and peripheral neuropathy.

Arterial inflammation is segmental, necrotizing, and transmural, leading to aneurysms and thrombosis.

The involved vessels are typically found at arterial bifurcations, spreading to veins but sparing venules. The most commonly affected organs are the kidney, heart, liver, and gastrointestinal tract, in that order. Pulmonary arteries are not involved. Inadequate blood flow leads to ischemia, ulcers, infarcts, atrophy, or hemorrhage.

Diagnosis relies on histopathological findings from organ biopsies or the demonstration of aneurysms in small to medium-sized arteries of the renal, hepatic, and visceral vasculature.

Untreated PAN has an extremely poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of only 10 to 20%. Common causes of death include gastrointestinal complications, such as bowel infarcts and perforation, as well as cardiovascular issues. Timely treatment is vital for improved outcomes.

Combining prednisone and cyclophosphamide has shown significant benefits in survival rates. Glucocorticoids alone may be sufficient for milder cases. In PAN cases associated with hepatitis B or C, antiviral therapy is combined with glucocorticoids and plasma exchange. Managing hypertension effectively can help reduce vascular complications. Despite successful treatment, relapses occur in approximately 10-20% of patients.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A factory worker working in a plastic pipe factory presented to the OPD with weight loss and right upper quadrant abdominal pain of 6 months duration. He had hepatomegaly. Further investigation revealed that most of the liver was replaced by a hemorrhagic tumor with extensive necrosis. What can be the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiosarcoma of the liver

The diagnosis is angiosarcoma of the liver.

Angiosarcoma of the liver is usually seen in individuals having occupational exposure to agents such as vinyl chloride, arsenic, or thorotrast. The gross specimen of the liver  shows greyish white lesions, with multiple reddish-brown hemorrhagic foci and several blood-filled spaces .

Option A: Cavernous hemangiomas appear as red-blue, soft nodules, usually less than 2 cm in diameter. Their clinical significance is that they might be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for metastatic tumors.

Option B: Metastatic carcinoma of the liver has a gross appearance that shows multiple nodular lesions of variable size, replacing much of the normal parenchyma.

Option D: Primary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a peak incidence around 20 to 40 years of age and is predominantly seen in men. The gross appearance shows unifocal or multifocal or diffusely infiltrative lesions that are paler than the surrounding tissue. The lesions may be greenish due to the presence of bile. Cirrhosis may be seen in about 50% of the cases. Intrahepatic metastases may be seen.

questions.text: Inhaled NO is used in:

Correct answer: A. Primary Pulmonary Artery Hypertension

It reduces pulmonary artery pressure without causing systemic hypotension, making it useful in primary pulmonary arterial hypertension.

It is not indicated for OSA, unstable angina, or erectile dysfunction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the accommodative amplitude of a patient with a near point at 20 cm and a far point at infinity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 D

The amplitude of accommodation for the above patient would be 5 dioptres.

Near point of accommodation (NPA) is the closest distance at which the near object is clearly focussed without blur.

Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum power of the lens that permits clear near vision without blur. Its unit is dioptre (D). The amplitude of accommodation is the reciprocal of near point of accommodation (NPA) in meters.

20 cm is 1/5th of a metre. Therefore, the accommodative amplitude is its inverse, that is, 5D.

Note:

The NPA is measured clinically using a scale device such as the Prince, Berens, or Royal Air Force (RAF) ruler.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Stain used in staining fungal elements:
questions.explanation: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) is a specialized histological stain used specifically to visualize fungal elements. It stains fungal cell walls (containing chitin) a deep black color against a light green background, providing excellent contrast. This makes it ideal for identifying fungi like Pneumocystis jirovecii, Histoplasma, or Aspergillus in tissue sections. Acid-fast stain (Option A) is primarily used for Mycobacteria (e.g., TB). Gram stain (Option B) is used for bacteria; while some fungi like Candida are Gram-positive, it is not the preferred or specific stain for broad fungal identification. Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) is another common fungal stain. Because GMS is the most specific and widely used stain among the choices for identifying the complex structures of various fungal species in clinical samples, it is the correct answer
questions.learning: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) is a specialized histological stain used specifically to visualize fungal elements. It stains fungal cell walls (containing chitin) a deep black color against a light green background, providing excellent contrast.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant presents with hypotonia and seizures. It was confirmed to be cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is accumulated in the brain in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long chain fatty acid

Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome or Zellweger's syndrome is characterized by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acid, abnormalities of synthesis of bile acids and a marked reduction of plasmalogens.

It occurs in individuals with a rare inherited absence of peroxisomes. It is due to mutations in genes encoding certain proteins called peroxins (involved in various steps of peroxisome biogenesis) in all tissues. They accumulate C26-C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissues and also exhibit a generalized loss of peroxisomal functions. It causes severe neurological symptoms and most patients die in the first year of life.
questions.learning: Long chain fatty acid Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome or Zellweger's syndrome is characterized by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acid, abnormalities of synthesis of bile acids and a marked reduction of plasmalogens.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A vegetable vendor with no prior criminal history went missing and was found dead a week later in an advanced state of decomposition. What methods can be used to identify the body in such a situation?
questions.explanation: In cases of advanced decomposition, many traditional methods of identification become unreliable. General recognition (Option A) is impossible as the facial features are destroyed. Fingerprints (Option D) are often lost due to skin "gloving" or putrefaction. While dental records (Option C) are a highly effective and standard method, they require a pre-existing dental chart for comparison, which a person like a "vegetable vendor with no history" may not have. DNA profiling is currently the most definitive and robust method for identifying decomposed remains. DNA can be extracted from stable tissues like the teeth or long bones (the femur) even a week or more after death. The profile can then be compared to a reference sample from the missing person's belongings or, more commonly, to DNA from living first-degree relatives. DNA profiling provides a scientific certainty of identification that is essential for legal and closure purposes in missing person cases
questions.learning: In cases of advanced decomposition, many traditional methods of identification become unreliable. General recognition (Option A) is impossible as the facial features are destroyed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A child under 5 years of age presents with a painless, soft, and fluctuant mass on the lateral side of the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless, soft, fluctuating mass on the lateral side of the neck in a child under 5 years is a classic description of a Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma). These are congenital malformations of the lymphatic system, most commonly found in the posterior triangle of the neck. They characteristically transilluminate brilliantly. A thyroglossal cyst (Option A) is a midline mass that moves with tongue protrusion. Cervical lymphadenopathy (Option C) is usually firmer and often associated with a history of infection or fever. A ranula (Option D) is a mucous extravasation cyst found on the floor of the mouth, though a "plunging" ranula can present in the neck. Cystic hygromas can occasionally grow rapidly if they bleed internally or become infected, potentially causing airway obstruction. While some small lesions may regress, the primary treatment for symptomatic or large cystic hygromas is surgical excision or sclerotherapy using agents like OK-432 or bleomycin to shrink the cysts
questions.learning: A painless, soft, fluctuating mass on the lateral side of the neck in a child under 5 years is a classic description of a Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Counter current mechanism is found in: i. Eye ii. Testis iii. Gut iv. Kidney v. Lungs
options: ii, iii, iv, v are correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ii, iii, iv, v are correct

A countercurrent mechanism occurs when two fluids flow in opposite directions, allowing efficient exchange of heat, gases, or solutes.

Sites where countercurrent mechanisms occur:

• Testis: Countercurrent heat exchange in the pampiniform plexus helps maintain testicular temperature lower than body temperature for spermatogenesis.
• Gut: Countercurrent blood flow in intestinal villi facilitates efficient nutrient absorption and exchange.
• Kidney: Countercurrent multiplier (Loop of Henle) and countercurrent exchanger (vasa recta) concentrate urine.
• Lungs: Countercurrent heat and moisture exchange occurs in the respiratory passages.

Eye does not have a classical countercurrent exchange system.
questions.learning: ii, iii, iv, v are correct A countercurrent mechanism occurs when two fluids flow in opposite directions, allowing efficient exchange of heat, gases, or solutes.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Order of appearance of rigor mortis:
options: Orbicularis oculi, facial muscles, thorax, upper limb
Orbicularis oculi, neck, facial muscles, upper limb, thorax
Neck, muscles of eyelid, upper limb, thorax
Neck, muscles of eyelid, facial muscles, thorax, upper limb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbicularis oculi, facial muscles, thorax, upper limb

The correct order is orbicularis oculi, facial muscles, thorax, and upper limb.

Nysten's rule describes the sequential onset of rigor mortis in various muscle groups.

Rigor mortis begins from the head and progresses down the body:

• The order of appearance of rigor mortis is heart (left chamber) → eyelids → muscles of the neck → lower jaw → muscles of the face → muscles of the chest(thorax) → upper limb → abdomen → lower limb → fingers and toes (proximo-distal progression)

It disappears in the same order of appearance.

Note that in option B, the upper limb is mentioned before thorax and hence is not the answer.
questions.learning: Orbicularis oculi, facial muscles, thorax, upper limb The correct order is orbicularis oculi, facial muscles, thorax, and upper limb. Nysten's rule describes the sequential onset of rigor mortis in various muscle groups.

questions.text: What is the function of utricle and saccule?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Linear acceleration

The function of utricle and saccule is linear acceleration.

Utricle and saccule which contain sensory epithelium called macula that are stimulated by linear acceleration and deceleration or gravitational pull during the head tilts.

The ampullated end of each semicircular canal contains a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium called crista ampullaris that respond to angular acceleration and deceleration.

Hearing is mediated by the organ of Corti on the basilar membrane of the inner ear.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady presents to the OPD with complaints of fatigue. On examination, there is pallor. Blood investigations showed a hemoglobin of 10g/dl, RBC count of 3 million cells/mm cube, MCV = 70 fL, MCH = 22 pg. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical findings are consistent iron deficiency anemia

This patient has microcytic (N: 82-96 fL) and hypochromic (N: 27-33 pg) anemia. The differential diagnoses of microcytic hypochromic anemia include iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, and anemia of chronic disease. Since there is reduced RBC count (normal 4.5 to 6.5 milllion/cubic mm), the best answer is Iron deficiency anemia.

The single best test to differentiate between various diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anemia is iron profile.  Low Ferritin and high TIBC( total iron binding capacity) is seen in Iron deficiency anaemia, while Thalassemia major has normal/high ferritin and low/normal TIBC.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following biomedical waste management methods is correct for the disposal of an expired tablet?
questions.explanation: Under the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, expired or discarded medicines (including tablets) are classified as pharmaceutical waste. These must be segregated into the Yellow bag. The mandated final disposal method for this category is incineration at temperatures exceeding to ensure complete chemical destruction. The Red bag (Option A) is for recyclable plastic waste like IV sets and catheters, usually disposed of via autoclaving. The Blue bag (Option B) is for glassware and metallic implants, treated by disinfection or recycling. Deep burial (Option C) in yellow bags is reserved for human anatomical waste in rural or remote areas without access to incinerators, but it is not the standard for chemical/pharmaceutical waste. Improper disposal of expired drugs can lead to environmental contamination and antibiotic resistance. Correct segregation ensures that toxic pharmaceutical components do not enter the general waste stream or water supply
questions.learning: Under the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, expired or discarded medicines (including tablets) are classified as pharmaceutical waste. These must be segregated into the Yellow bag.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor used to treat hypertension. This entire class of drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D/X). ACE inhibitors can cause severe fetal and neonatal injury, including renal failure, limb deformities, lung hypoplasia, and fetal skull defects (ACE inhibitor fetopathy). Paracetamol (Option B) is generally considered the safest analgesic and antipyretic throughout pregnancy. Ranitidine (Option C) is an H2-blocker commonly used for acid reflux and is not contraindicated. Cefixime (Option D) is a third-generation cephalosporin and is a safe antibiotic choice for infections during pregnancy. For pregnant women with hypertension, safer alternatives like Labetalol, Methyldopa, or Nifedipine should be used instead of ACE inhibitors or ARBs. This pharmacological knowledge is vital for preventing iatrogenic fetal harm. Any woman of childbearing age prescribed an ACE inhibitor must be counseled about its teratogenic risks and the need for reliable contraception
questions.learning: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor used to treat hypertension. This entire class of drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D/X).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit due to severe sepsis caused by a ruptured abdominal abscess. She has been receiving high-dose intravenous corticosteroids for hypotension management over the past three days. On examination, she is alert but appears critically ill. Laboratory results are as follows: • TSH: 1.2 µU/mL (normal range: 0.4–4.0 µU/mL) • Free T4: 1.1 ng/dL (normal range: 0.8–1.8 ng/dL) • Free T3: 0.6 pg/mL (normal range: 2.0–4.4 pg/mL) Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Euthyroid sick syndrome

Euthyroid sick syndrome (non-thyroidal illness syndrome) occurs in severe systemic illness such as sepsis, trauma, or critical illness. Thyroid gland function is normal, but peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism is altered. Typical laboratory pattern:

• ↓ Free T3 (most common finding)
• Normal or ↓ T4
• Normal or slightly ↓ TSH

Mechanism:

• Severe illness and stress hormones (e.g., cytokines, glucocorticoids)
• ↓ peripheral conversion of T4 → T3 due to reduced 5′-deiodinase activity
questions.learning: Euthyroid sick syndrome Euthyroid sick syndrome (non-thyroidal illness syndrome) occurs in severe systemic illness such as sepsis, trauma, or critical illness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What test is not used for testing olfaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arnold stick test

Arnold stick test is not a test used for olfaction.

Tests used for olfaction are as follows:

1. Smell diskettes are used as a screening test for olfaction. Reusable diskettes are used with the application of 8 different odorants. A questionnaire with illustrations is used to score the patient.
2. The University of Pennsylvania smell identification test (UPSIT) is a commercially available, self-administered test used to assess the function of an individual's olfactory system via smell identification. It uses microencapsulated odorants, which are released on scratching standardized odor-impregnated test booklets.
3. The 12-item version of UPSIT, also known as the cross-cultural smell identification test (CC-SIT), is useful for quantifying smell loss when less time is available. This test serves as a means to reliably assess olfactory function in less than 5 minutes.
4. The Sniffin' sticks test is a new test of nasal chemosensory performance based on pen-like odor-dispensing devices.
questions.learning: Arnold stick test Arnold stick test is not a test used for olfaction. Tests used for olfaction are as follows: 1.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: HPV infection is most commonly associated with which type of cancer?
questions.explanation: High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly with HPV-16, is strongly linked to a rising subset of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas, including those of the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV is also classically associated with cervical and other anogenital malignancies. Lung cancer (Option A) is primarily associated with environmental factors like smoking and radon rather than viral infection. Stomach cancer (Option C) is most commonly linked to Helicobacter pylori infection. Esophageal cancer (Option D) risk factors typically include alcohol, smoking, and Barrett’s esophagus. Because HPV selectively targets the mucosal surfaces of the oropharynx, it has become a major causative factor for these specific head and neck cancers
questions.learning: High-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly with HPV-16, is strongly linked to a rising subset of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas, including those of the tonsils and base of the tongue.

Correct answer: C. Omeprazole, Clarithromycin and Metronidazole

H. pylori peptic ulcer requires triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics.

• Colonizes gastric mucosa
• Produces urease → ammonia → mucosal damage

• Causes:

• Chronic gastritis
• Peptic ulcer

Standard Triple Therapy

• PPI (e.g., Omeprazole)
• Clarithromycin
• Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole if penicillin allergy)

Important Tests:

• Urea breath test
• Stool antigen test

Complications of H. pylori:

• Gastric carcinoma
• MALT lymphoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most effective treatment for a 3-year-old child diagnosed with 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation: Accommodative esotropia is a type of inward eye turn caused by excessive convergence that occurs when a farsighted (hyperopic) child tries to clear their vision. In a 3-year-old child, the most effective and standard first-line treatment is refractive correction (Option D) with full-cycloplegic spectacles. By correcting the underlying farsightedness, the need for excessive accommodation—and thus the associated convergence/crossing—is eliminated, often straightening the eyes immediately. Orthoptic exercises (Option A) may have a limited role in convergence insufficiency but are not the primary treatment for accommodative crossing. Surgery (Option B) is contraindicated as the primary treatment because the crossing is refractive; operating could lead to an outward turn (exotropia) later. Relieving prisms (Option C) are used for small paralytic deviations rather than primary childhood esotropia. Therefore, prescription glasses are the definitive and most appropriate clinical intervention for this condition. Early correction is essential to prevent permanent amblyopia and ensure the development of normal binocular vision
questions.learning: Accommodative esotropia is a type of inward eye turn caused by excessive convergence that occurs when a farsighted (hyperopic) child tries to clear their vision.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of death in patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory Failure

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic progressive interstitial lung disease characterized by:

• Diffuse pulmonary fibrosis
• Progressive stiffening of lung tissue
• Impaired gas exchange

The pathology pattern is called: Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP).

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causes progressive restrictive lung disease with worsening hypoxemia.

The most common terminal event is respiratory failure due to extensive fibrotic destruction of lung parenchyma.

Pulmonary hypertension and lung cancer may occur but are less common immediate causes of death.

Aspiration pneumonia is not the typical terminal event in IPF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman presented with claudication in the forearm, transient loss of vision, and abdominal pain. Femoral pulses were weak. Fundus examination revealed retinal hemorrhages. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Takayasu arteritis

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with claudication in the forearm, weak femoral pulses, abdominal pain and transient loss of vision is suggestive of Takayasu arteritis.

A patient with polyarteritis nodosa will present with abdominal pain, renal involvement, and hypertension. Musculoskeletal symptoms present as arthralgia, arthritis, or myalgia. The presence of large vessel symptoms such as claudication in the forearm and weak femoral pulses makes the diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa unlikely (option A).

Takayasu arteritis is a chronic inflammatory medium- and large- vessel vasculitis that commonly affects adolescents and young females. It mainly involves the aortic arch and its branches. Depending on the artery occluded, patients present with the following symptoms:

• Subclavian artery (most common) - pain, numbness, claudication, and weak or absent radial pulses on the affected side
• Common carotid artery - visual symptoms, syncope, and stroke
• Abdominal aorta, superior mesenteric artery, and coeliac axis - abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
• Renal artery - hypertension and renal failure
• Aortic arch or root - aortic insufficiency, heart failure
• Pulmonary artery - atypical chest pain, dyspnea
• Coronary artery - chest pain, myocardial infarction
• Iliac artery - Leg claudication, weak/absent pulses in the periphery

Patients also have constitutional symptoms such as malaise, fever, night sweats, weight loss, etc.

Investigations:

1. Lab reports reveal an elevated ESR level, anemia, and elevated immunoglobulin levels.
2. Arteriography is done as a confirmatory test.

Treatment includes glucocorticoid therapy, methotrexate, immunotherapy with anti-TNF agents, and surgery of the stenosed vessels.

Other options:

Option A: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is necrotizing arteritis of the medium-sized blood vessels. It can affect the skin, peripheral nerves, renal vessels, mesenteric vessels, heart, and brain. Lungs are usually spared in PAN.The disease initially starts with non-specific symptoms like fever, malaise, arthralgia, and myalgia. Later, depending on the artery involved, patients may develop the following symptoms:

• Skin findings - ulcers, digital gangrene, subcutaneous nodules, and livedo reticularis
• Renal arteries - hypertension and renal failure
• Mesenteric arteries - abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, bleeding, and a bowel perforation

Patients can have musculoskeletal symptoms (arthralgia, myalgia) and mononeuritis multiplex.

Option B: Thromboangiitis obliterans, also known as Buerger's disease, is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder involving medium- and small-sized vessels in the distal extremities. It is most frequently seen in male smokers less than 40 years of age.The patient presents with a triad of claudication of the distal extremities, Raynaud's phenomenon, and migratory superficial vein thrombophlebitis. Proximal pulses (brachial artery, femoral artery, popliteal artery) are normal. But distal pulses (radial, ulnar, tibial artery) are weak/absent.

Option D: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis affecting small- and medium-sized vessels. It occurs most commonly in elderly males. Patients can present with non-constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and musculoskeletal pain. Renal involvement is very common (79%) in the form of glomerulonephritis, which can rapidly progress, causing renal failure. It is also associated with mononeuritis multiplex, alveolar hemorrhage (present with hemoptysis as 1st symptom), and cutaneous vasculitis. Lab findings include anemia, raised ESR and or CRP, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and ANCA positive in 75% of patients,
questions.learning: Takayasu arteritis — The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with claudication in the forearm, weak femoral pulses, abdominal pain and transient loss of vision is suggestive of Takayasu arteritis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tarsal bone marked by the arrow in the given X-ray of the right foot.
questions.explanation: The arrow points to the navicular bone, a wedge-shaped tarsal bone situated on the medial aspect of the midfoot. It is anatomically located between the talus (proximally) and the three cuneiform bones (distally). On a dorsoplantar or oblique X-ray, its position on the medial side is highly distinctive. The cuboid bone (Option B) is located on the lateral aspect of the foot. The intermediate cuneiform (Option C) and lateral cuneiform (Option D) are located distal to the navicular and articulate with the metatarsals. Accurate identification of midfoot tarsal bones is essential for diagnosing fractures and dislocations in trauma cases. Based on the medial position between the talar head and the cuneiforms, the bone indicated is the navicular

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has well-developed breasts but lacks axillary and pubic hair. Examination reveals normal female external genitalia. Pelvic ultrasound shows an absent uterus, and karyotyping reveals a 46,XY genotype. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Androgen insensitivity syndrome

A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea, well-developed breasts, absent axillary and pubic hair, normal female external genitalia, absent uterus, and a 46XY karyotype is most likely to have androgen insensitivity syndrome.

Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is an X-linked recessive disorder in which the androgen receptors are absent, scanty, or fail to respond to testosterone. As a result, resistance to androgens may be complete, and female external genitalia are found. The individual has a genetic makeup of 46XY but is phenotypically a female. The Wolffian duct fails to develop because of the absence of testosterone receptors. Testes produce Mullerian-inhibiting factors, so the Müllerian system fails to develop. However, the lower portion of the vagina derived from the sinovaginal bulb appears as a dimple of 1–2 cm in length. AIS can be present in two forms:

* Complete variety

* Incomplete variety

Clinical presentation of complete AIS includes:

* Primary amenorrhea and/or infertility

* Well-developed breasts

* ↓ growth of axillary and pubic hair

* Female-looking external genitalia, short and blind vagina, absent uterus and fallopian tubes. The testes may be located in the labia, inside the abdominal cavity, or within the inguinal canal.

In partial AIS, a few receptors respond to testosterone, resulting in variable clinical features. Some patients present at birth with ambiguous genitalia, and chromosome study reveals XY chromosomes, while others present at puberty, with lack of virilization in a boy or signs of virilization in a girl with primary amenorrhoea.

Investigations:

* Karyotype: 46, XY.

* Serum testosterone: within normal limits for males.

* Serum E2 level:  more than normal for males.

* Serum LH level: normal or slightly raised.

Other options:

Option A: MRKH( Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser)-Mullerian agenesis : Present with similar findings but with 46,XX karyotype.

Option B: Sweyer syndrome or pure gonadal dysgenesis occurs as a result of a mutation in the SRY gene (karyotype: 46,XY). This leads to underdeveloped, dysgenetic gonads. They have normal uterus and vagina with no breast development.

Option D: Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO). In Turner's syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis causes primary ovarian failure that is hypogonadism. The clinical picture of amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck, widely spaced nipples, and lack of secondary sexual characteristics is seen in Turner's syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a newborn admitted to the NICU with respiratory distress and passage of meconium from the umbilicus, which anatomical structure is responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of meconium or fecal discharge from the umbilicus in a newborn is pathognomonic for a vitelline fistula. This condition results from a complete failure of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct to obliterate during embryological development. Normally, this duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac and closes by the eighth week of gestation. Persistence of the entire duct creates a direct communication between the ileum and the umbilicus, allowing intestinal contents (meconium) to leak out. The mesonephric duct (Option A) is involved in the development of the male reproductive system. The allantois (Option B) and its remnant, the urachus (Option C), connect the bladder to the umbilicus; their persistence leads to a urachal fistula, characterized by the discharge of urine, not meconium. Therefore, the specific nature of the discharge (fecal/meconium) definitively identifies the vitelline fistula as the responsible anatomical abnormality in this infant

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents to OPD with lethargy, weakness, and persistent low back pain. Blood investigations revealed normochromatic anemia, hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis showed an M spike. Prognosis is determined by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum Beta 2 microglobulin + Albumin

The clinical scenario of a 40-year-old female who presented to OPD with lethargy, weakness, and persistent low back pain, with blood investigations revealing normochromic anemia, hypercalcemia, and serum protein electrophoresis showing M spike, is consistent with the diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma (MM). Serum Beta 2 microglobulin + Albumin is used to determine the prognosis of the MM.

The International Staging System (ISS) is used to assess prognosis in patients with multiple myeloma, with serum β₂-microglobulin serving as the most important prognostic marker.

Multiple myeloma: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* Disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia, Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions, Renal failure, Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation

Evidence of end-organ damage caused by the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder: (CRAB features)

* Hypercalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL

* Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL

* Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL

* Bone lesions: One or more lytic lesions on bone radiographs, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET-CT).

Any one or more of :

* Plasma cells in the bone marrow clonally proliferated up to 60% or higher

* The ratio of serum involved to uninvolved free light chains of 100 or greater

* Greater than one focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least >5 mm in size

Treatment includes a combination of lenalidomide/thalidomide (immunomodulatory agents), bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor), and dexamethasone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The movements at the ____________ joint permit a person to look to the right and left.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atlanto-axial

The movements at the atlanto-axial joint allow a person to look left and right.

The atlanto-axial joints include 3 synovial joints:

• Median atlanto-axial joint- The central pivot joint between the dens of the axis and a ring formed by the anterior arch and transverse atlantal ligament
• Lateral atlanto-axial joints- Plain synovial joints between lateral masses of atlas and upper facets of the body of axis

Movements at the atlanto-axial joint almost exclusively is rotation around the axis, which help side-to-side rotation of the head. The normal range of atlanto-axial rotation is about 40°.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A breastfed infant presents with lethargy, hepatomegaly, and cataract formation. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of lethargy, hepatomegaly, and cataracts shortly after starting breastfeeding is diagnostic of classic galactosemia. This inborn error of metabolism is caused by a deficiency in Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT/GALPUT). The deficiency leads to a toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver and galactitol in the lens of the eye. Untreated cases risk severe mental retardation, E. coli sepsis, and liver failure. Galactokinase deficiency (Option A) causes isolated cataracts without the severe hepatic or systemic symptoms seen here. Aldolase B deficiency (Option C) results in hereditary fructose intolerance, which presents after the introduction of fruit or formula containing sucrose rather than breastfeeding. Fructokinase deficiency (Option D) is a benign condition known as essential fructosuria. Management of classic galactosemia requires the immediate and permanent withdrawal of galactose and lactose from the infant's diet
questions.learning: The clinical triad of lethargy, hepatomegaly, and cataracts shortly after starting breastfeeding is diagnostic of classic galactosemia. This inborn error of metabolism is caused by a deficiency in Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT/GALPUT).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sudden heat sensation associated with profuse sweating and flushing over the past several months. She has irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition. Which of the following is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum FSH level

In women with vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, flushing, night sweats) and irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition, the most useful laboratory test—if confirmation is required—is serum FSH. Ovarian follicular depletion leads to reduced estrogen production, causing loss of negative feedback and a rise in FSH (typically >25–30 IU/L, though levels fluctuate during perimenopause).

High-Yield Points

• Most menopausal women do not require laboratory confirmation if they are >45 years with typical symptoms.
• If testing is indicated (e.g., younger women or uncertain diagnosis), FSH is the preferred investigation.
• FSH ↑, LH ↑ (less marked than FSH), Estradiol ↓.
• Progesterone is not useful for diagnosing menopause.
questions.learning: Serum FSH level — In women with vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, flushing, night sweats) and irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition, the most useful laboratory test—if confirmation is required—is serum FSH.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with a movement disorder marked by hand tremors, along with cognitive decline and emotional disturbances. Given the age of onset and the combination of motor and neuropsychiatric features, which diagnosis best fits this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The triad of an adult-onset movement disorder (tremors/chorea), cognitive decline (dementia), and emotional/psychiatric symptoms is diagnostic for Huntington's disease. This is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an unstable expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene. Imaging characteristically shows atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen. Parkinson’s disease (Option A) primarily presents with resting tremors and bradykinesia, while cognitive decline usually occurs much later in the disease course. Friedreich Ataxia (Option B) typically presents in childhood or adolescence with cerebellar signs and limb weakness. Alzheimer’s disease (Option C) is primarily a disorder of memory and cognition, and while motor symptoms can occur, they are not the presenting feature in a 50-year-old. The progressive nature and the specific combination of "choreiform" movements and psychiatric changes are the defining features of Huntington's, making genetic testing for CAG repeats the confirmatory step
questions.learning: The triad of an adult-onset movement disorder (tremors/chorea), cognitive decline (dementia), and emotional/psychiatric symptoms is diagnostic for Huntington's disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Extra mammary Paget's disease is commonly seen in the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vulva

Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

Extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) can be primary or secondary.

• Primary EMPD is more common and occurs in the absence of an underlying malignancy, thought to arise from intraepidermal parts of apocrine glands or from pluripotent cells from the epidermis.
• Secondary EMPD arises from an underlying adnexal carcinoma or internal malignancy due to the epidermotropic spread of malignant cells from the underlying tumor.

Visceral malignancies associated with EMPD are carcinomas of the colon, rectum, bladder, urethra, cervix, and prostate. The patient presents with well-defined, moist, erythematous scaly plaques and severe pruritis. Lichenification and excoriations may also be seen.

Diagnosis is confirmed by punch, wedge, or excisional skin biopsy. A systemic workup should also be done to identify any underlying malignancy and they include colonoscopy, cystoscopy, colposcopy, and pelvic examination with pap smear in females.

Treatment:

• Mohs microscopic surgery with 5 cm margin clearance
• Radiotherapy
• Topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod
• Chemotherapy
• Photodynamic therapy

The given image below shows extramammary Paget's disease of the vulva.
questions.learning: Vulva Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A male patient diagnosed with tuberculosis took complete treatment. Sputum examination was done after the completion of the intensive and the continuation phases. It was found to be negative. What is the status of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cured

The negative sputum examination at the end of the treatment implies the status of the patient is cured.

Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The disease mainly affects the lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis.

A bacteriologically confirmed TB case is one in which the biological specimen tests positive on smear microscopy and culture. A clinically diagnosed TB case is one that is diagnosed as an active TB case by a clinician, who has decided to give the patient a full course of TB treatment.

There are two phases in the treatment of TB. The intensive phase lasts for 2 months and four drugs are used. They are isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. The continuation phase lasts for 4 months, where isoniazid is given along with rifampicin and Ethambutol.

After the completion of anti-tubercular treatment, the sputum/culture is tested and one of the outcomes given below is assigned to the patient:

• Cured - A TB patient whose smear or culture turned negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion
• Treatment completed - A TB patient who completed treatment without any failure, but has no record to show that sputum smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion were negative; it may be either because tests were not done or because results are unavailable
• Treatment failed - A TB patient whose sputum smear or culture is still positive after treatment for 5 months or more
• Lost to follow-up - A TB patient who did not start treatment or whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more
• Died - A TB patient who dies before starting or during the course of treatment for any reason
• Not evaluated - A TB patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned; this includes cases "transferred out" to another treatment unit and cases for whom the treatment outcome is unknown to the reporting unit whose treatment I interrupted
questions.learning: Cured — The negative sputum examination at the end of the treatment implies the status of the patient is cured. Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: IV anesthetic agent that causes adrenocortical suppression is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate inhibits 11-β-hydroxylase, blocking cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, leading to dose-dependent adrenocortical suppression. Even a single dose can reduce steroid production for 6–12 hours. Because of this, it is avoided in septic or critically ill patients who depend on adequate stress-hormone response.
questions.learning: Etomidate Etomidate inhibits 11-β-hydroxylase, blocking cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, leading to dose-dependent adrenocortical suppression. Even a single dose can reduce steroid production for 6–12 hours.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A pus swab has been sent for microbiological examination to your lab. After testing the sample, how will you discard it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow bin

The used pus swab should be discarded in the yellow colour bin as it is clinical laboratory waste.

Microbiology, biotechnology, and clinical laboratory waste are collected in autoclave-safe bags. They must be pre-treated before disposal by incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial.
questions.learning: Yellow bin — The used pus swab should be discarded in the yellow colour bin as it is clinical laboratory waste. Microbiology, biotechnology, and clinical laboratory waste are collected in autoclave-safe bags.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A baby presents to the OPD and the findings are shown in the image below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Capillary hemangioma

The image shows a capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular area. A capillary haemangioma is the most common tumor of the orbit and periorbital area in childhood.

Hemangioma is a benign tumor caused by the abnormal growth of blood vessels. Types of hemangioma are:

* Capillary hemangioma (most common)

* Juvenile/ strawberry hemangioma

* Cavernous hemangioma

* Pyogenic hemangioma

Capillary hemangioma may present as small isolated lesions or large masses that can cause visual impairment (due to mechanical ptosis and the resulting sensory deprivation amblyopia), systemic effects (severe thrombocytopenia), or exist as part of PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial lesions, Cardiac abnormalities, Eye or Endocrine abnormalities)

30% of lesions resolve by the age of 3 years and about 75% by the age of 7. On histology, they show thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma as shown below.

Indications for treatment are:

* Visual (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion, strabismus)

* Cosmesis

* Optic nerve compression

* Exposure keratopathy

Capillary hemangioma regresses spontaneously very often. Treatment options include:

* Beta-blockers- oral propranolol, topical timolol.

* Steroids- intralesional triamcinolone or betamethasone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids.

* Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine- for steroid-resistant sight-threatening lesions

* Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser.

Option A: Port wine stain is a congenital low-flow vascular malformation that may occur anywhere in the body and does not fade away with time. Visually they appear as partially or completely blanchable, pink to red or reddish brown patches, mostly on the head and neck. This lesion is associated with syndromes such as Sturge-Weber syndrome and occult spinal dysraphism.

Option B: Cavernous hemangiomas are large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma. They are infiltrative and involve deep structures. They do not regress spontaneously. Von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas. These vascular lesions are commonly found in the cerebellum, brain stem, retina, pancreas, and liver.

Option C: Salmon patches or naevus simplex (as shown below) are small, ill-defined, pink-colored macules commonly seen over the glabella, eyelids, upper lip, and nuchal area, which develop due to vascular ectasia. It is a common vascular birthmark and disappears within 1 year.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Gonadal growth corresponds with
questions.explanation: According to Scammon's curves of systemic growth, the growth of the gonadal (genital) system remains very slow during childhood but undergoes a massive surge during puberty. This pattern of rapid acceleration in adolescence closely corresponds with the skeletal system's growth spurt during the same period. In contrast, the brain (Option A) and nervous system reach nearly adult size by age 6. Lymphoid growth (Option C) actually peaks around age 10–12 (reaching 200% of adult size) before regressing after puberty. Dental growth (Option D) follows a different developmental timeline related to primary and permanent tooth eruption. Understanding these distinct growth patterns is essential for pediatricians and endocrinologists to assess if a child's development is proceeding normally. The synchronization of skeletal maturation (bone age) and genital development is a hallmark of the pubertal process, making the skeletal system the most appropriate correlate for gonadal growth among the listed options
questions.learning: According to Scammon's curves of systemic growth, the growth of the gonadal (genital) system remains very slow during childhood but undergoes a massive surge during puberty.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pairs of parasites and associated clinical manifestations are correct? 1. Ancylostoma duodenale — Anemia 2. Ascaris lumbricoides — Löffler Syndrome 3. Loa loa — Katayama Fever 4. Trichinella spiralis — Myositis Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

1. Ancylostoma duodenale → Anemia — Correct

• Hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa and cause chronic intestinal blood loss, leading to iron-deficiency anemia.

2. Ascaris lumbricoides → Löffler syndrome — Correct

• Larvae migrate through the lungs, causing transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia (Löffler syndrome).

3. Loa loa → Katayama fever — Incorrect

• Katayama fever is associated with acute schistosomiasis, particularly Schistosoma mansoni and S. japonicum.
• Loa loa causes Calabar swellings and can cause episodic angioedema.

4. Trichinella spiralis → Myositis — Correct

• Larvae encyst in skeletal muscle, producing myalgia, muscle inflammation, and eosinophilia.
questions.learning: Ancylostoma duodenale → Anemia — Correct • Hookworms attach to the intestinal mucosa and cause chronic intestinal blood loss, leading to iron-deficiency anemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with vision problem in his right eye. On examination IOP of his right eye is 50 mmHg and left eye is 16 mm Hg. Slit lamp examination shows presence of flare cells in anterior chamber and cataractous lens in the right eye. What is the diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phacolytic glaucoma

Phacolytic glaucoma is a lens-induced secondary open-angle glaucoma caused by leakage of high-molecular-weight lens proteins from a hypermature (cataractous) lens.

• Elderly patient with mature/hypermature cataract
• Very high IOP (e.g., 50 mmHg)
• Open anterior chamber angle
• Flare and cells in anterior chamber (due to macrophages ingesting lens proteins)
• Pain and decreased vision

Pathophysiology:

• Leakage of lens proteins → macrophage response
• Protein-laden macrophages block trabecular meshwork
• Leads to raised IOP

Why not others:

• Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Due to intumescent (swollen) lens causing angle closure

• Malignant glaucoma:

• Aqueous misdirection, shallow anterior chamber, usually post-surgery

• Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis:

• Chronic mild uveitis, not associated with very high IOP and hypermature lens

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis. While dissecting Calot's triangle, a lateral injury to the common bile duct occurred, leading to significant bile leakage into the operative field. The surgeon has limited experience in laparoscopy. What is the most appropriate intraoperative management step at this stage?
options: Continuing laparoscopic repair of the common bile duct
Placing a drainage tube in subhepatic space
Closing the abdomen and taking the patient for ERCP and biliary stenting
Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Converting the laparoscopic surgery to open surgery and placing a T-tube through the injured common bile duct

Bile duct injury is one of the most serious complications of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, most commonly occurring during dissection of Calot’s triangle due to misidentification of biliary anatomy. In this case:

• Lateral injury to the common bile duct (CBD)
• Significant bile leak
• Surgeon has limited laparoscopic experience

The safest management is to convert to open surgery and repair the injury over a T-tube, which decompresses the biliary tree and allows postoperative cholangiography.

Why not the other options?

• A. Continue laparoscopic repair of common bile duct: Not advisable in an inexperienced surgeon; increases the risk of further injury and stricture.
• B. Place only a drainage tube in subhepatic space: Inadequate for a recognized CBD injury.
• C. Close abdomen and perform ERCP and biliary stenting later: ERCP is useful for postoperative leaks but recognized major intraoperative bile duct injuries should be addressed immediately.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the left third intercostal space, and a pistol-shot sound is noted over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of an early diastolic murmur at the left third intercostal space (Erb’s point) is the classic auscultatory finding for Aortic Regurgitation (AR). Palpitations result from the high stroke volume and forceful ventricular contractions. The "pistol shot sound" (Traube's sign) refers to loud systolic sounds heard over the femoral arteries, which is a classic peripheral sign of chronic severe AR caused by the wide pulse pressure. Aortic stenosis (Option B) presents with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. Tricuspid regurgitation (Option C) and Mitral regurgitation (Option D) both typically produce holosystolic murmurs rather than diastolic ones . Other signs of AR include a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse and De Musset’s sign (head nodding with each heartbeat). Diagnosis is confirmed with echocardiography to visualize the regurgitant jet and assess left ventricular function. Aortic regurgitation leads to volume overload of the left ventricle and eventual failure if left untreated
questions.learning: The presence of an early diastolic murmur at the left third intercostal space (Erb’s point) is the classic auscultatory finding for Aortic Regurgitation (AR).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Erythropoietin is produced by:

1. Kidney
2. Liver
3. Spleen
4. Lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2

Erythropoietin is produced mainly by kidney and liver.

In adults, approximately 85% of erythropoietin is produced by the kidneys, while 15% is synthesized by the liver. Both of these organs possess the mRNA necessary for erythropoietin production. Although erythropoietin can be found in the spleen and salivary glands, these tissues lack the mRNA required for its synthesis, indicating that they do not produce the hormone.

Erythropoietin is secreted by interstitial cells in the peri-tubular capillary bed of the kidneys and by perivenous hepatocytes in the liver. It is also generated in the brain, where it provides a safeguarding effect against excitotoxic harm caused by hypoxia; and in the uterus and oviducts, where it is stimulated by estrogen and seems to facilitate estrogen-driven angiogenesis.
questions.learning: 1,2 Erythropoietin is produced mainly by kidney and liver. In adults, approximately 85% of erythropoietin is produced by the kidneys, while 15% is synthesized by the liver.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA is present in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitochondria

Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells. They have their own small circular DNA, known as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which encodes a limited number of genes.

mtDNA is inherited maternally and is essential for the synthesis of certain proteins involved in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation.

The presence of DNA in mitochondria is a key characteristic that distinguishes them from other cellular structures.

Other Options:

*

Lysosome: Cellular organelles containing enzymes that degrade cellular waste and foreign substances.

*

Cytoplasm: Region within a cell that surrounds the nucleus and organelles. While some cellular activities occur in the cytoplasm, DNA is primarily housed in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.

* Endoplasmic reticulum: Complex network of membranes involved in protein synthesis, lipid metabolism, and calcium storage. It does not typically contain DNA.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with fever of 38.5 °C and fundal spots. CBC shows a leukocyte count of 20,000/cu mm, and blood cultures have been sent. In this scenario, how many minor Duke’s criteria are met for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: The Duke’s criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis by identifying a combination of major and minor criteria. In this patient, only minor criteria can be assessed based on the given information. The following three minor criteria are fulfilled: 1. Predisposing condition: The patient is an intravenous drug user, which is a known risk factor for infective endocarditis. 2. Fever ≥ 38°C: The patient has a temperature of 38.5°C, meeting the fever criterion. 3. Immunologic phenomenon: The presence of fundal spots (Roth spots) indicates an immunologic manifestation. Although blood cultures have been sent, their results are not yet available, so microbiological evidence cannot be counted at this stage. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 6 :Too many; only three criteria present (C) 4 : Assumes positive blood culture, which is not given (D) 2 : Misses one valid criterion
questions.learning: The Duke’s criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis by identifying a combination of major and minor criteria. In this patient, only minor criteria can be assessed based on the given information.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis for the given image?
questions.explanation: The laparoscopic image displays characteristic "beading" or nodules on the fallopian tubes, which are highly suggestive of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB). FGTB often presents with caseous nodules, tubercles, and the "Sharma’s python sign" (alternating constriction and dilation). Regarding the distractors, a normal fallopian tube (Option B) is thin-walled and smooth without any nodules. A hydrosalpinx (Option C) appears as a fluid-distended, thin-walled "sausage-shaped" tube but lacks the caseous nodules seen here. Endometriosis (Option D) typically shows "powder-burn" lesions or "chocolate cysts" on the ovaries rather than diffuse white nodules on the tubes. Because genital TB is a leading cause of infertility in endemic regions and presents with these specific laparoscopic features, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The laparoscopic image displays characteristic "beading" or nodules on the fallopian tubes, which are highly suggestive of female genital tuberculosis (FGTB).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, increased salivation, bradycardia (pulse rate 55/min), and markedly reduced plasma cholinesterase levels (50 U/ mL), suggestive of cholinergic toxicity. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for managing this condition?
options: Benztropine tropine The patient is exhibiting a "cholinergic crisis," likely due to organophosphate or carbamate poisoning. The constellation of symptoms—often remembered by the acronym DUMBELS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation)—results from the overstimulation of muscarinic receptors. Atropine is the definitive pharmacological antidote. It acts as a competitive muscarinic antagonist, effectively blocking the excessive acetylcholine and reversing life-threatening symptoms like bradycardia and bronchoconstriction. Neostigmine (Option A) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that would actually worsen the crisis. Epinephrine (Option C) can treat bradycardia but does not address the underlying cholinergic excess. Benztropine (Option D) is a centrally acting anticholinergic used for Parkinson's but lacks the peripheral potency required for systemic poisoning management. Therefore, titration of intravenous Atropine until "atropinization" (indicated by clear lungs and dry secretions) is the standard emergency protocol.
questions.explanation: The patient is exhibiting a "cholinergic crisis," likely due to organophosphate or carbamate poisoning. The constellation of symptoms— often remembered by the acronym DUMBELS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation)—results from the overstimulation of muscarinic receptors. Atropine is the definitive pharmacological antidote. It acts as a competitive muscarinic antagonist, effectively blocking the excessive acetylcholine and reversing life- threatening symptoms like bradycardia and bronchoconstriction. Neostigmine (Option A) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that would actually worsen the crisis. Epinephrine (Option C) can treat bradycardia but does not address the underlying cholinergic excess. Benztropine (Option D) is a centrally acting anticholinergic used for Parkinson's but lacks the peripheral potency required for systemic poisoning management. Therefore, titration of intravenous Atropine until "atropinization" (indicated by clear lungs and dry secretions) is the standard emergency protocol. questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a limbal scar, a deep anterior chamber, and absence of the lens on slit-lamp examination. He reports difficulty with both distance and near vision. His vision improves to 6/9 with a +11D lens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aphakia

Aphakia is the absence of the crystalline lens, leading to marked hypermetropia.

• Deep anterior chamber
• Absence of lens on slit lamp
• Severe blurred vision (distance + near)
• Improved with high plus lens (+10 to +12 D)

Clinical clues in question:

• Limbal scar → previous surgery/trauma
• +11 D correction → classic for aphakia

Why not others:

• Pseudophakia → artificial IOL present
• Subluxation → lens still visible
• Presbyopia → only near vision affected

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient on chronic furosemide therapy for heart failure develops volume depletion. Laboratory studies show elevated serum bicarbonate. What is the primary mechanism underlying this acid-base disturbance?
options: Direct inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Aldosterone-mediated H⁺ secretion in the distal nephron secondary to volume contraction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aldosterone-mediated H⁺ secretion in the distal nephron secondary to volume contraction

Furosemide-induced volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The resulting aldosterone excess increases H⁺ secretion (in exchange for Na⁺/K⁺ reabsorption) at the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, generating "contraction metabolic alkalosis." Option A describes the mechanism of acetazolamide, which causes metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis; C and D are unrelated mechanisms not implicated in loop diuretic-induced alkalosis.
questions.learning: Aldosterone-mediated H⁺ secretion in the distal nephron secondary to volume contraction Furosemide-induced volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy. What type of prevention is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tertiary prevention

The clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with cancer and undergoing chemotherapy points towards tertiary prevention, as it is already diagnosed and treatment aimed at reducing the number and impact of complications.

The tertiary level of prevention signifies intervention in the late pathogenesis phase. Tertiary prevention can be defined as "all measures available to reduce or limit impairments and disabilities, minimize suffering caused by existing departures from good health, and promote the patient's adjustment to irremediable conditions". Examples include occupational and physical therapy in burns patients and cardiac rehabilitation in post-myocardial infarction patients.

Other options:

Option A: Secondary prevention includes early disease detection and targets healthy-looking individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. Secondary prevention is defined by an intervention that halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is an example of secondary prevention aimed at diagnosing cervical cancer in its subclinical state before progression.

Option C: Primordial prevention prevents the emergence or development of risk factors in population groups or countries where they have not appeared yet through individual and mass education. For example lifestyle modifications such as eating patterns and physical exercise to prevent obesity in later years.

Option D: Primary prevention is the action taken before the onset of the disease to prevent the possibility that a disease will ever occur. Here, intervention is initiated in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease. It is accomplished by population strategy and high-risk strategy. Examples of primary prevention are immunization and sanitising hands.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with lethargy, vomiting, and poor feeding following a period of prolonged fasting. Laboratory evaluation shows hypoglycemia with low ketone levels and mild hepatomegaly, suggesting a disorder of fat metabolism. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease)
questions.explanation: This presentation is the classic clinical hallmark of MCAD deficiency, the most common fatty acid beta-oxidation defect. Normally, during fasting, the body switches to fat oxidation to produce energy and ketones. In MCAD deficiency, the inability to break down medium-chain fats leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and fat accumulation in the liver (mild hepatomegaly). Her's disease (Option A) causes fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, but ketone production remains normal because fat oxidation is intact. Hereditary fructose intolerance (Option C) occurs after fructose ingestion, not fasting. Von Gierke disease (Option D) presents with severe hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, but ketones are typically normal or even high rather than low. Thus, the specific failure to produce ketones during a hypoglycemic fasting state identifies MCAD deficiency
questions.learning: This presentation is the classic clinical hallmark of MCAD deficiency, the most common fatty acid beta-oxidation defect. Normally, during fasting, the body switches to fat oxidation to produce energy and ketones.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital external auditory atresia

Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) is useful in congenital external auditory canal atresia.

Bilateral aural atresia presents with failed audiological testing and requires early bone conduction hearing aids, one of which is BAHA, which combines a sound processor with a small titanium fixture implanted behind the ear and allows the bone to transfer sound to a functioning cochlea rather than via the middle ear – a process known as direct bone conduction.

It consists of three parts:

* An innermost titanium fixture in the bone

* A middle abutment

* An outer hearing aid fixed to the abutment

Bone-anchored Hearing Aids are used:

* When air-conduction (AC) hearing aid cannot be used:

* People who have chronic inflammation or infection of the ear canal are associated with discharge and cannot wear standard “in the ear” air-conduction hearing aids.

* Children with malformed or absent outer ear and ear canals as in microtia or canal atresia.

* In Conductive or mixed hearing loss, e.g. otosclerosis and tympanosclerosis where surgery is contraindicated

* In single-sided deafness

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial lemniscus is a continuation of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fasciculus gracilis

Medial lemniscus is a continuation of fasciculus gracilis.

Posterior column–medial lemniscal pathway:

First-order axons carrying discriminative touch and vibration sensations enter the dorsal horn and continue traveling upward in the posterior white column as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

Fibers of these fasciculi synapse on the second-order neurons of the ipsilateral nuclei gracilis and cuneatus in the medulla oblongata, respectively.

Axons of these second-order neurons then cross over as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus in the contralateral medulla.

These second-order axons ascend through the brainstem to reach the third-order neuronal cell bodies in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Axons from the third-order neurons then project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to reach the primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue and polyuria. On examination, vital signs are stable, and an HbA1c test is performed. What is the HbA1c cut-off percentage used to define well-controlled diabetes?
questions.explanation: As established in Question 35, Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) is the standard for monitoring long-term glycemic control. For the majority of non-pregnant adults with diabetes, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and other global guidelines recommend an HbA1c cut-off of less than 7.0% to define controlled diabetes. Maintaining this level significantly reduces the risk of long-term microvascular complications like retinopathy and nephropathy. A cut-off of 6.5% (Option B) is used as a diagnostic threshold to define the presence of diabetes, rather than the target for control. 6.0% (Option A) is near the normal range and may be too strict for many patients, increasing the risk of hypoglycemia. 7.5% (Option D) is considered suboptimal control. These targets must be individualized; for example, elderly patients or those with short life expectancy may have a more relaxed target (e.g.,). However, "7.0%" is the standard "general" goal for effective diabetes management

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with meningitis with a history of fever for 4 days and erythematous rashes on the chest. There was no history of travel and tick bite. His CSF findings showed increased protein, normal glucose, mild lymphocytosis and few RBCs. Which of the following is the most likely organism to cause this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Entero virus

Meningitis with normal glucose, increased protein, and mild lymphocytosis is suggestive of viral meningitis, most probably by an Enterovirus.

Coxsackieviruses are typical enteroviruses. Two groups of Coxsackie viruses A and B, are known. Aseptic meningitis may be caused by a majority of group A and all group B viruses. A maculopapular rash may be present. The disease can also occur as epidemics.

CSF findings in Viral meningitis:

• A mild increase in CSF protein/pressure
• Normal glucose

• Mild increase in lymphocytes in CSF.

Other options:

West Nile virus is endemic in certain regions in North America. But there is no history of travel mentioned in the clinical scenario above. Current hotspots in North America are the California Central Valley, southwestern Arizona, southern Texas, and Louisiana, which have both compatible climates and avian reservoirs for the disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following shows functional assessment of B1 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RBC Transketolase

Erythrocyte (RBC) transketolase test is the most widely used method for the functional assessment of thiamine deficiency.

Thiaminediphosphate is a co-enzyme for transketolase. Therefore, in thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, the RBC transketolase activity is reduced. When thiamine diphosphate is added in-vitro to erythrocyte lysate, activation of apo-transketolase is suggestive of B1 deficiency.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding oligohydramnios: 1. It is defined on USG when maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than 5 cm. 2. It is defined on USG when AFI is less than 5 cm. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

Oligohydramnios refers to decreased amniotic fluid volume and is associated with increased maternal and fetal morbidity. It is diagnosed by ultrasonography using either the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) or the Single Deepest Vertical Pocket (SDVP/Maximum Vertical Pocket, MVP).

Why is B correct?

• 1. It is defined on USG when maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than 5 cm. ✗

• Oligohydramnios is defined when the Single Deepest Vertical Pocket (SDVP/MVP) is <2 cm, not <5 cm.

• 2. It is defined on USG when AFI is less than 5 cm. ✓

• AFI <5 cm is the standard ultrasound definition of oligohydramnios.
