questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman earning ₹20,000 undergoes a tubectomy. How many days of leave is she entitled to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 14 days

Under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended), a woman who undergoes a tubectomy operation is entitled to 2 weeks (14 days) of paid leave immediately following the procedure.

• The salary mentioned (₹20,000) does not change the duration of leave.

Why not the other options?

• A. 4 days: Incorrect; no such provision exists.
• B. 7 days: Incorrect; 7 days is not the leave entitlement for tubectomy under the Maternity Benefit Act.
• D. 10 days: Incorrect; the statutory leave is 14 days.
questions.learning: 14 days Under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended), a woman who undergoes a tubectomy operation is entitled to 2 weeks (14 days) of paid leave immediately following the procedure. • The salary mentioned (₹20,000) does not change the duration of leave.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the status of the marked individual?
options: Has a disease of chronic origin
questions.explanation: In standard pedigree notation, an individual symbol (square for male, circle for female) placed within brackets indicates that the person has been adopted. Specifically, dashed brackets usually signify that the individual was "adopted in" from another family, whereas solid brackets indicate the individual was "adopted out" to a different family. Chronic or curable diseases (Options B and C) would be represented by specific shading or filling of the symbol, not by brackets. Twins (Option D) are indicated by connecting siblings to a single point on the lineage line with a diagonal bar or triangle. Therefore, the use of brackets around a pedigree symbol is strictly reserved to denote the adoption status of that family member, ensuring accurate genetic history tracking
questions.learning: In standard pedigree notation, an individual symbol (square for male, circle for female) placed within brackets indicates that the person has been adopted.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a diabetic patient presenting with a fungal infection involving the sinuses and periorbital region, along with significant visual impairment, which medication would be the most appropriate choice for treatment?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario—a diabetic patient with invasive fungal sinusitis and periorbital involvement (Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis)—is a surgical and medical emergency. Liposomal Amphotericin B is the gold-standard, first-line systemic antifungal agent for this condition. It provides broad-spectrum coverage against Mucorales and other aggressive molds while having a better safety profile regarding nephrotoxicity than conventional amphotericin. Itraconazole (Option A) and Ketoconazole (Option C) are oral azoles that lack the necessary potency for acute, invasive, life-threatening fungal infections of this nature. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option D) have no activity against fungi and would only be useful for secondary bacterial infections. The "notable visual impairment" suggests orbital invasion, which necessitates immediate intravenous therapy alongside aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue. Therefore, intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin B is the definitive and life-saving pharmacological intervention for this patient
questions.learning: The clinical scenario—a diabetic patient with invasive fungal sinusitis and periorbital involvement (Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis)—is a surgical and medical emergency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about red blood cells in Sickle cell anemia:
options: Low mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility
High mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility
Low mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility
High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility

Sickle RBCs are rigid → break easily (↑ mechanical fragility) but resist swelling (↓ osmotic fragility).

Correct answer is D because sickled RBCs are rigid and easily damaged while passing through microcirculation, leading to increased mechanical fragility and hemolysis.

HbS polymerization

↓

Rigid sickle RBC

↓

↓ Deformability

↓

↑ Mechanical damage

↓

Hemolysis

(1) Nucleated red cell, (2) target cell, and (3) irreversibly sickled red cell.

Due to dehydration and increased intracellular Hb concentration, sickled RBCs show decreased osmotic fragility compared to normal RBCs.

Thus, sickle cells are mechanically fragile but relatively resistant to osmotic lysis.

| Feature | Sickle Cell | Spherocytosis

| ------- | ----------- | -------------

| Shape | Sickle | Spherical

| Mechanical fragility | ↑ | ↑

| Osmotic fragility | ↓ | ↑

| Reason | Rigid | Less surface area

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness and blurred vision that worsen with exertion and toward the end of the day, along with ptosis on examination. Her symptoms improve significantly after an edrophonium test. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. The key diagnostic feature in this case is the "fatigability"—symptoms that worsen with exertion and towards the end of the day. MG commonly affects the ocular muscles first, presenting as ptosis (drooping eyelids) and diplopia (blurred/double vision). The positive edrophonium (Tensilon) test, where a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor leads to temporary improvement in muscle strength, is highly suggestive of MG. Option A (Lambert Eaton) is a paraneoplastic syndrome where strength often improves with repeated effort, unlike MG. Option C (Guillain-Barré) is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculopathy presenting with ascending paralysis. Option D is a respiratory condition. MG is caused by antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Treatment involves pyridostigmine, immunosuppressants, and occasionally thymectomy, as the disease is often associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. The key diagnostic feature in this case is the "fatigability"—symptoms that worsen with exertion and towards the end of the day.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department after an accidental burn. She has burns involving her right upper limb, the entire right lower limb, and the entire anterior and posterior abdomen. Using the Rule of Nines, what is the estimated total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns?
questions.explanation: The Wallace Rule of Nines is used to estimate the total body surface area (TBSA) burned in adults. Applying it step by step: 1. Right upper limb = 9% 2. Entire right lower limb = 18% 3. Anterior abdomen = 9% 4. (Anterior trunk is 18%; abdomen represents half of it) Posterior abdomen = 9% (Posterior trunk is 18%; abdomen represents half of it) Total TBSA burned: 9% + 18% + 9% + 9% = 45% Therefore, the estimated burned TBSA is 45%, making Option (A) correct. Why others are incorrect: 28% underestimates by excluding major areas. 60% and 70% overestimate by incorrectly counting full trunk or extra limbs. Accurate TBSA estimation is crucial for fluid resuscitation, commonly calculated using the Parkland formula: Half is given in the first 8 hours, and the rest over the next 16 hours. Incorrect estimation can lead to fluid overload or hypovolemic shock

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with a right upper limb nerve injury. On examination, the patient can flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: The ability to perform flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints is primarily the function of the lumbrical muscles. The lumbricals are innervated by the median and ulnar nerves. If the patient can still perform these specific movements, it indicates that the median and ulnar nerves are largely intact. However, the radial nerve (Option D) is responsible for the extension of the MCP joints and the wrist. Radial nerve injury, common in humeral shaft fractures following road traffic accidents, leads to "wrist drop" and the inability to extend the MCP joints. The median nerve (Option A) primarily controls thumb opposition and finger flexion. The anterior interosseous nerve (Option B), a branch of the median, controls the "OK" sign (flexion of the thumb IP and index distal IP joints). The ulnar nerve (Option C) controls most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Therefore, the clinical preservation of lumbrical-mediated movements while experiencing upper limb trauma most likely points to a radial nerve injury
questions.learning: The ability to perform flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints is primarily the function of the lumbrical muscles.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman visits the doctor with pain and weakness in her right forearm and hand for several months. Two years ago, she had a fracture in her ulnar shaft and a dislocation of her radial head that required surgery. On examination, there is mild tenderness a few centimeters distal to the lateral epicondyle. She has significant weakness when trying to extend her right middle finger and radial deviation on extension of the wrist. Sensation is normal. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior interosseous nerve

PIN is:

• A branch of radial nerve → Purely motor
• Supplies:

• Finger extensors, Thumb extensors, Extensor carpi ulnaris

Normally wrist extension uses:

• Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)
• Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
• Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)

In PIN palsy:

• ECU is weak
• ECRL still works (supplied before PIN branches out from radial nerve.

So wrist extends but deviates radially.

A) Anterior interosseous nerve

• Motor branch of median nerve → Affects flexors (FPL, FDP index)
• Difficulty in making OK sign
• No extensor weakness

B) Superficial radial nerve

• Pure sensory nerve → Causes numbness dorsum of hand
• No motor weakness

D) Ulnar nerve

• Affects intrinsic hand muscles → Clawing of 4th and 5th digits
• No extensor weakness

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the Dystrophin protein completely absent?
questions.explanation: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a frameshift mutation in the DMD gene. This results in a complete absence of the protein dystrophin (Option B). Dystrophin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the muscle fiber's sarcolemma; its absence leads to progressive muscle necrosis and weakness. In Becker's Muscular Dystrophy (Option A), the mutation allows for the production of a truncated, partially functional dystrophin protein, resulting in a milder phenotype. Myasthenia gravis (Option C) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (Option D) are autoimmune disorders affecting the neuromuscular junction (acetylcholine receptors or calcium channels) and do not involve dystrophin defects. Therefore, the absolute lack of this critical structural protein is pathognomonic specifically for Duchenne's. This leads to the characteristic clinical findings of pseudohypertrophy and Gowers' sign in young boys
questions.learning: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a frameshift mutation in the DMD gene. This results in a complete absence of the protein dystrophin (Option B).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the method used to assess the relative risk (RR)?
questions.explanation: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the strength of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is defined as the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed group to the incidence in the non-exposed group. Because a cohort study begins with exposed and non-exposed individuals and follows them forward in time to observe the development of disease, it allows for the direct calculation of incidence, and thus, the Relative Risk. A Case-control study (Option A) uses the Odds Ratio (OR) because it looks backward and cannot determine true incidence. A Randomized Controlled Trial (Option C) also allows for RR calculation but is an experimental rather than observational design. A Cross-sectional study (Option D) measures prevalence rather than incidence. Therefore, the cohort study is the classic observational method for determining RR
questions.learning: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the strength of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is defined as the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed group to the incidence in the non-exposed group.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The most appropriate description of vasomotor reversal of Dale is
options: Repeated administration of ephedrine decreases its effect on blood pressure
A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on administration of adrenaline.
High dose of acetylcholine after pretreatment with atropine produces increase in blood pressure and heart rate
Increase in pulse pressure is produced by intravenous administration of isoprenaline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on administration of adrenaline.

A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on the administration of adrenaline is the most appropriate description of the vasomotor reversal of Dale. (Option B)

Vasomotor reversal of Dale is a blockade of alpha (α1) followed by stimulation of beta (β2) receptors.

Normally, a high dose of epinephrine injected produces α1 mediated rise in BP followed by β2 mediated fall in BP.

Vasomotor reversal of Dale: Administration of adrenaline after administration of α blockers(phentolamine) produces only a fall in BP. This is because the α mediated response is abolished and hence, only the β-mediated response is seen, i.e., a fall in BP.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis has multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting. Which of the following metabolic abnormality is likely to be seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypochloremic, hypokalemic alkalosis

Multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) lead to hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis.

Emesis causes loss of gastric fluid containing H+ ions, leading to the release of bicarbonate into the bloodstream. Without normal neutralization in the small intestine, metabolic alkalosis develops. This is the generation phase of alkalosis.

Volume depletion during vomiting hinders the urinary excretion of bicarbonate. This is due to reduced glomerular filtration, increased proximal tubule resorption of sodium and bicarbonate, and elevated aldosterone levels promoting bicarbonate resorption and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct. This is the maintenance phase.

Loss of chloride ions in the gastric acid leads to hypochloremia.

Hydrogen ions exit from the cells in exchange for potassium leading to hypokalemia. Loss of fluid due to excessive vomiting activates the RAAS pathway. This worsens hypokalemia as the aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for the secretion of K+ and H+ ions into the urine.  The loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH, resulting in paradoxical aciduria.

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus resulting in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. It is common between 3 and 6 weeks of age. First-born male infants are at the highest risk.

Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting. It is associated with hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. The nipple sign is produced by the double-layered hypertrophic mucosa that protrudes into the stomach. The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is therefore called the cervix sign.

The image below shows the cervix and nipple sign seen in IHPS:

Management includes the correction of metabolic abnormality prior to surgery. Administering 5% dextrose and 0.45% saline with added potassium at a rate of 150-175 mL/kg per 24 hours can correct the fluid deficit in infants. Monitoring urine output (>2 cc/kg/h) is important to ensure successful rehydration.

The hypertrophic pylorus is surgically corrected by Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic approach). It involves splitting the pyloric muscle while preserving the underlying submucosa.
questions.learning: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic alkalosis Multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) lead to hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following refractive errors is associated with the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Astigmatism

The given image is a Sturm's conoid. It represents the configuration of a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic (toric) surface and helps in understanding the optics of regular astigmatism.

Astigmatism is a type of refractive error that occurs when light rays enter the eye at different planes and converge at different points forming focal lines.

When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface (surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points and form two focal lines. The shape of a bundle of light rays at different points is as follows:

For the given Sturm's conoid,

• At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays.
• At point B (first focus), vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging; so, it will be a horizontal straight line.
• At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging, and horizontal rays are still converging.
• At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged; so, we get a perfect circle called the circle of least diffusion.
• At point E, a vertical oval is formed.
• At point F (second focus), a vertical straight line is formed
• At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/ prolate ellipse.
• The focal interval of Sturm refers to the distance between two foci (B and F).

The image is clearest or least confusing as point D, the circle of least confusion/ circle of diffusion. The circle of diffusion lies at the mid-point of this interval.

• Option A: Presbyopia is a refractive error caused by the loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens, leading to difficulty in focusing on near objects. Presbyopia is not associated with Sturm's conoid.
• Option C: Hypermetropia, or farsightedness, is a refractive error in which the eye does not focus incoming light properly, causing near objects to appear blurry. It is not associated with Sturm's conoid.
• Option D: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error in which distant objects appear blurry because the eye focuses light in front of the retina rather than on it. Myopia is not associated with Sturm's conoid.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antiarrhythmic drugs is contraindicated in a patient with interstitial lung disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

Amiodarone is contraindicated in a patient with interstitial lung disease.

The most serious adverse effect during chronic amiodarone therapy is pulmonary fibrosis, which can be rapidly progressive and fatal. Underlying lung disease, doses of 400 mg/day or more, and recent pulmonary insults such as pneumonia appear to be risk factors for this condition.

Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug.

The side effects of amiodarone include:

• Pulmonary fibrosis
• Hypotension, depressed ventricular function
• Torsades de pointes
• Corneal microdeposits
• Hepatotoxicity
• Neuropathies
• Photosensitivity
• Thyroid dysfunction
questions.learning: Amiodarone Amiodarone is contraindicated in a patient with interstitial lung disease. The most serious adverse effect during chronic amiodarone therapy is pulmonary fibrosis, which can be rapidly progressive and fatal.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is a ssRNA virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus belonging to the Paramyxoviridae family.

• Genome: Negative-sense ssRNA
• Family: Paramyxoviridae
• Transmission: respiratory droplets
•

Common diseases:

o    Bronchiolitis (most common cause in infants)

o    Pneumonia in young children and elderly

•

Characteristic feature: Formation of syncytia (multinucleated giant cells) in respiratory epithelium

Why not others:

• Human papillomavirus (HPV): double-stranded DNA virus
• Adenovirus: double-stranded DNA virus
• Parvovirus: single-stranded DNA virus (only ssDNA virus)

questions.text: A 52-year-old woman diagnosed with carcinoma cervix stage 2B was advised radiotherapy. Which of the following statements regarding radiotherapy is false? (NEET PG 2020)
options: Point B is 3 cm lateral to point A
Point A is 2 cm above the external os and 5 cm lateral to the internal uterine canal
Point A receives a dose of 7000 cGy
Point B receives a dose of 6000 cGy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Point A is 2 cm above the external os and 5 cm lateral to the internal uterine canal

Point A

• A point 2 cm lateral and 2 cm superior to the external cervical os.
• Represents the anatomical location of the ureter.
• The total dose to point A should not exceed 8000 cGy.

Point B

• Represents a dose to the pelvic wall.
• The dose to point B is about 25 – 30% of the dose to point A (4500 – 6500 cGy)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of 1971, up to what maximum gestational age is medical termination of pregnancy legally permitted?
questions.explanation: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act was significantly amended in 2021 (updating the 1971 act). Under the current legal framework in India, the maximum gestational age for MTP has been increased to 24 weeks for certain categories of women. These categories include survivors of sexual assault, rape victims, minors, and women with disabilities or mental illness. For standard cases up to 20 weeks, the opinion of one doctor is required; for the 20-24 week window, the approval of two registered medical practitioners is mandatory. Termination beyond 24 weeks is generally only permitted in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities as determined by a State-level Medical Board. Options A, B, and D do not represent the primary legal thresholds defined by the modern act. Therefore, 24 weeks is the current definitive maximum age for the broad application of the law
questions.learning: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act was significantly amended in 2021 (updating the 1971 act). Under the current legal framework in India, the maximum gestational age for MTP has been increased to 24 weeks for certain categories of women.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A gym owner notices that individuals who consume iced tea during workouts appear to lose more weight. What type of relationship does this observation suggest?
questions.explanation: A spurious relationship is a mathematical relationship in which two variables have no direct causal connection, yet it may be wrongly inferred that they do, usually due to the presence of a third, unseen factor (a confounding variable). In this scenario, drinking iced tea doesn't cause weight loss. Instead, individuals who are disciplined enough to work out regularly (the real cause of weight loss) might also happen to prefer iced tea. The observed association between iced tea and weight loss is coincidental or influenced by the workout itself. A relative relationship (Option B) isn't a standard term in this context. A direct relationship (Option C) would mean iced tea chemically causes weight loss. An indirect relationship (Option D) would mean iced tea leads to another factor that then causes weight loss. Recognizing spurious correlations is vital in medical research to avoid drawing false conclusions about treatments or lifestyle habits. Researchers use randomized controlled trials to eliminate these confounding variables and establish true causality
questions.learning: A spurious relationship is a mathematical relationship in which two variables have no direct causal connection, yet it may be wrongly inferred that they do, usually due to the presence of a third, unseen factor (a confounding variable).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman with secondary amenorrhea shows high FSH/LH and AMH 0.05. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Premature ovarian failure

Primary Ovarian Insufficiency is defined as: Loss of ovarian function before 40 years of age

It results in amenorrhea, estrogen deficiency, and elevated gonadotropins.

| Hormone | Level

| ------- | -----

| FSH | ↑ High

| LH | ↑ High

| Estrogen | ↓ Low

| AMH | ↓ Very low

AMH reflects ovarian reserve. Very low AMH suggests depleted follicles.

Clinical Features

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Secondary amenorrhea | Loss of ovulation

| Infertility | No follicular development

| Hot flashes | Estrogen deficiency

| Vaginal dryness | Hypoestrogenism

Causes of Premature Ovarian Failure

| Cause | Example

| ----- | -------

| Genetic | Turner syndrome

| Autoimmune | Autoimmune oophoritis

| Iatrogenic | Chemotherapy / radiotherapy

| Idiopathic | Most common

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which government program is designed to provide health checkups and services for children aged 0–18 years, with special attention to out-of-school children?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is the specific national initiative designed for the early screening and management of children from birth up to 18 years. Crucially, it targets children enrolled in government and government-aided schools as well as out-of-school children through Anganwadi centers. The program screens for the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays. Janani Suraksha Yojana (Option B) is a maternal health scheme promoting institutional birth. Navjaat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (Option C) focuses exclusively on basic newborn care and resuscitation. The Mid day meal program (Option D) provides nutritional support but only to children attending school. RBSK ensures a continuum of care by referring identified cases to District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs) for free treatment. This universal screening is a major public health effort to reduce the burden of childhood morbidity and disability, particularly among marginalized populations who may not have regular access to healthcare or education
questions.learning: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is the specific national initiative designed for the early screening and management of children from birth up to 18 years.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meatoplasty

The surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal is meatoplasty.

Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of a crescent-shaped portion of conchal cartilage to widen the external auditory meatus. It is performed in combination with all canal wall-down procedures like modified radical and radical mastoidectomies, for easy access to the mastoid cavity for periodic inspection and cleaning.

It is also done as an isolated procedure in elderly people with sagging auricles. A sagging auricle causes obstruction to the meatus leading to the retention of wax and difficulty in hearing.

Other options:

Option B: Tympanoplasty is the surgical reconstruction to correct damage in the middle ear and restore the integrity of the tympanic membrane for improved hearing. It is ossicular reconstruction only or ossicular reconstruction with myringoplasty.

Option C: Myringoplasty refers to the reconstruction of the tympanic membrane only.

Option D: Otoplasty is the correction of external ear/deformities of the pinna.
questions.learning: Meatoplasty — The surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal is meatoplasty. Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of a crescent-shaped portion of conchal cartilage to widen the external auditory meatus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 61-year-old man with distal esophageal adenocarcinoma located 5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction is scheduled for curative resection. The surgical team plans an esophagectomy with a right thoracotomy and laparotomy, followed by intrathoracic anastomosis. Which of the following operative approaches is being described?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ivor-Lewis esophagectomy

Ivor–Lewis esophagectomy is the preferred surgical approach for distal and mid-esophageal cancers, especially adenocarcinoma near the gastroesophageal junction.

Key components of Ivor–Lewis procedure

• Two-incision approach:

o Laparotomy (abdominal phase)

o Right thoracotomy (thoracic phase)

• Gastric mobilization and creation of gastric conduit

• Intrathoracic esophagogastric anastomosis

Indications

• Distal esophageal carcinoma

• Gastroesophageal junction tumors

• Good oncologic exposure with mediastinal lymphadenectomy

Comparison with other approaches

• Transhiatal esophagectomy (THE): abdominal + cervical incision, no thoracotomy, cervical anastomosis

• McKeown (three-stage): laparotomy + right thoracotomy + cervical incision, cervical anastomosis

• Left thoracoabdominal: older approach for distal tumors

Advantages of Ivor–Lewis

• Better visualization of thoracic esophagus

• Adequate lymph node clearance

• Lower cervical anastomotic leak risk than McKeown
questions.learning: Ivor-Lewis esophagectomy Ivor–Lewis esophagectomy is the preferred surgical approach for distal and mid-esophageal cancers, especially adenocarcinoma near the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: On which principles does the mask provided below operate?
questions.explanation: The image displays a Venturi mask, which is a high-flow oxygen delivery system. Its operation is based on the Bernoulli principle (Option C) . According to this principle, as a gas (oxygen) passes through a narrow orifice at a high velocity, it creates a local area of low pressure. This low pressure "entrains" or pulls in a precise amount of room air through side ports. By varying the size of the orifice, the mask can deliver a fixed, accurate FiO2 to the patient. The Bohr effect (Option A) refers to the shift in hemoglobin's oxygen affinity due to . Boyle's law (Option B) relates pressure and volume of a gas. Mapleson's circuit (Option D) refers to different breathing system configurations rather than a physics principle for air entrainment. Therefore, the Bernoulli principle is the definitive physical law that allows the Venturi mask to provide consistent oxygen concentrations regardless of the patient's breathing pattern
questions.learning: The image displays a Venturi mask, which is a high-flow oxygen delivery system. Its operation is based on the Bernoulli principle (Option C) .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with obstructive lung disease is on salmeterol and tiotropium but continues to have breathlessness and frequent exacerbations. Which treatment option would be most appropriate for her current condition?
questions.explanation: The patient has COPD with persistent breathlessness and frequent exacerbations despite optimal bronchodilator therapy (LABA + LAMA). This suggests advanced disease, where addressing chronic hypoxemia becomes crucial. Long-Term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT) is indicated in such patients as it: 1. Improves oxygenation 2. Reduces dyspnea 3. Decreases frequency of exacerbations 4. Improves survival in hypoxemic COPD patients Why other options are incorrect: (A) Nebulization with LAMA + LABA: Already on these drugs; changing the route provides only symptomatic relief, not long-term benefit (C) Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV): Used in acute respiratory failure, not stable outpatient management (D) Pneumococcal Vaccine: Preventive measure; does not treat current breathlessness or hypoxemia Thus, the most appropriate next step is LTOT, which addresses the underlying hypoxia and disease severity
questions.learning: The patient has COPD with persistent breathlessness and frequent exacerbations despite optimal bronchodilator therapy (LABA + LAMA). This suggests advanced disease, where addressing chronic hypoxemia becomes crucial.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old unmarried woman complained of missed periods. She always had regular menstrual cycles. The pelvic examination is normal. What is the next step of management for this patient?
options: Reassure her that it’s normal to have delayed period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Beta HCG estimation

The first step to do if a woman misses her period is to rule out pregnancy. Beta-HCG estimation is the next step.

The most common test used for this purpose is the urine pregnancy test (UPT). Serum beta HCG can detect a pregnancy as early as 5 days before the first missed period.

Amenorrhoea is the absence of menstruation.

* It is a symptom and not a disease entity.

* Amenorrhea can be physiological or pathological.

* Primary amenorrhea is defined as no menstruation by age 15.

* Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses for 6 or more months or the length of 3 cycles after the establishment of regular menstrual cycles. The most common cause of secondary amenorrhea is pregnancy.

Pearl PF1534: Beta hCG in pregnancy

The pattern of beta hCG :

First detectable in plasma 7 to 9 days post-LH surge

⇓

Doubles every 2 days

⇓

Peaks at 8 to 10 weeks of gestation(~100 IU/mL)

⇓

Begins to decline at 10 to 12 weeks

⇓

Plateau at 16 weeks till term

* Higher maternal plasma hCG levels- Multifetal pregnancy, erythroblastosis fetalis, gestational trophoblastic disease, Down syndrome.

* Lower hCG plasma levels -early pregnancy wastage and ectopic pregnancy.
questions.learning: Beta HCG estimation — The first step to do if a woman misses her period is to rule out pregnancy. Beta-HCG estimation is the next step.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following MRI imaging techniques is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T2 MRI

The MRI shows CSF as bright/hyperintense while white matter is dark and grey matter is white, hence this is a T2 weighted MRI image.

T1 weighted image

* It is one of the basic MRI pulse sequences.

* The difference in the appearance of various tissues is due to their different T1 relaxation times.

* CSF has a long T1 time and appears dark.

T2 weighted images:

* It is also a basic MRI pulse sequence.

* It is based on the T2 relaxation time of the tissues.

* CSF appears bright in these images.

Short tau inversion recovery(STIR):

* It is a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fat.

* The imaging sequence is identified by observing the fat tissues and fluid-filled spaces.

* Fluids like CSF appear bright and fat appears dark.

Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR):

* It is also a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fluids.

* Fluids like CSF appear dark and pathological processes appear bright.

* It would appear as a fluid suppressed T2 image.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the process of breaking the clavicle during delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cleidotomy

Cleidotomy is the process of fracturing the clavicle using an instrument to free the anterior shoulder. It is usually done for a dead fetus (shown below).

It is a method of management of labor in the case of shoulder dystocia. Shoulder dystocia occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or on the sacral promontory respectively.

Management of labor in case of shoulder dystocia is as follows:

* First line:

* McRoberts maneuver (flexion and abduction of the thigh)

* Second line:

* Woods corkscrew maneuver (Rotate the posterior shoulder to 180o in a corkscrew fashion)

* Third line:

* Zavanelli maneuver: It involves the replacement of the fetal head into the pelvis followed by cesarean delivery. (Option C)

* Cleidotomy

* Symphysiotomy: The intervening symphyseal cartilage and ligamentous supports are cut to widen the symphysis pubis. (Option B)

Option A: Craniotomy is not used in the management of shoulder dystocia. It is an operation in which a small hole is made in the skull or a piece of bone from the skull is removed to show part of the brain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old child was brought to the clinic with a history of difficulty in feeding and failure to thrive. On examination, the child is floppy, 48 cm in length and weighs 2.8 kg. There is generalized hypotonia, macroglossia and hepatomegaly. The chest x-ray of the child is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pompe's disease

The child with a clinical history of difficulty feeding and failure to thrive with generalised hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and chest x-ray findings of massive cardiomegaly suggest a diagnosis of Pompe's disease.

Pompe's disease is a glycogen storage disorder(type II) caused by a deficiency of lysosomal acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase) which leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of the liver (hepatomegaly), skeletal muscles in the form of large vacuoles (hypotonia and weakness), cardiac muscles (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). The child generally dies by the age of 2 years due to cardiac failure. The adult form presents with muscle dystrophies.

Laboratory findings show elevated levels of serum creatine kinase (CK), aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Urine glucose tetrasaccharide, a glycogen breakdown metabolite, is a reliable biomarker for disease severity and treatment response. Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant enzyme a-glucosidase alfa (Myozyme).

Given below is the image of muscle biopsy showing glycogen-positive vacuoles.

Other options:

Option A- Ebstein's anomaly is the teratogenic effect of maternal lithium consumption which causes a cyanotic heart disease in the newborn with atrialization of the right ventricle and conduction defects. The chest X-ray will show a box-shaped enlargement of the right atrium and pulmonary oligemia.

Option C- Transposition of great vessels is cyanotic congenital heart disease where there is a switch in the position of two main arteries i.e. pulmonary artery and aorta. X-ray shows of egg-on-string appearance with pulmonary plethora.

Option D- Von Gierke disease occurs due to a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. Patients present commonly in 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.
questions.learning: Pompe's disease — The child with a clinical history of difficulty feeding and failure to thrive with generalised hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and chest x-ray findings of massive cardiomegaly suggest a diagnosis of Pompe's disease.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl has intense cravings for food. She eats large amounts of food, which is followed by self-induced vomiting. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulimia nervosa

The probable diagnosis in the given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting is bulimia nervosa.

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder, often seen in young women. It is characterized by binge-eating episodes, followed by inappropriate, compensatory measures to stop weight gain, like self-induced vomiting, laxative abuse, diuretics, enema, and emetic abuse. These binge-eating episodes occur at least once a week and are present for at least 3 months. The patient fears gaining weight and has a relentless drive to be thin.

The weight is normal in most patients with bulimia nervosa. However, few patients may either be overweight or underweight. There is a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

Treatment modalities are cognitive behavioral therapy, psychotherapy, and antidepressants such as fluoxetine.

Other options:

Option A: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder that is often seen between the ages of 10 and 30. Typical features are self-induced starvation, voluntary and unhealthy reduction in weight, intense drive for thinness, and fear of becoming obese. These symptoms are usually present for at least a period of 3 months. Associated features can include depression, anxiety, amenorrhea in females, hypothermia, and bradycardia.

Option C: Atypical depression is a type of depression characterized by mood reactivity, which is brightening of the mood in response to positive events; significant weight gain or increase in appetite; hypersomnia; leaden paralysis; and/or interpersonal rejection sensitivity, resulting in significant social or occupational impairment.

Option D: Binge-eating disorder is the most common eating disorder. It is characterized by rapid intake of abnormally large quantities of food over a short period of time, even when not hungry. There are feelings of guilt about the eating episodes, but these patients do not compensate in any way following the episodes of binge.
questions.learning: Bulimia nervosa — The probable diagnosis in the given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting is bulimia nervosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustains a deep laceration over the scalp. Separation of the wound margins occurs due to injury to which of the following layers of the scalp?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)

The galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) is the third layer of the scalp and connects the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. When this layer is lacerated, the opposing pull of these muscles causes wide separation (gaping) of the wound margins, especially in wounds that run transversely across the scalp. Therefore, scalp lacerations involving the galea require meticulous repair to restore the continuity of the aponeurosis.

• The patient has a deep scalp laceration with separation of wound margins.
• This occurs because the galea aponeurotica is divided, allowing:

• Frontalis muscle to pull the anterior flap forward.
• Occipitalis muscle to pull the posterior flap backward.

• The resulting tension causes the wound to gap widely

| Layer Injured | Clinical Finding

| ------------- | ----------------

| Skin | Superficial abrasion/laceration

| Dense connective tissue | Profuse bleeding

| Galea aponeurotica | Gaping scalp wound

| Loose areolar tissue | Spread of infection; “black eye” after scalp injury

| Pericranium | Limited subperiosteal hematoma (cephalohematoma)

Why not the other options?

• A. Skin: Provides the external covering of the scalp but does not cause wound gaping when injured.
• B. Dense connective tissue: Contains blood vessels and nerves anchored by fibrous septa. Injury causes profuse bleeding but not wound separation.
• D. Loose areolar tissue: Known as the “danger area of the scalp” because infection can spread through emissary veins to the intracranial venous sinuses. Injury to this layer does not cause gaping of the wound.
questions.learning: Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) — The galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) is the third layer of the scalp and connects the frontalis and occipitalis muscles.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The functioning of the thyroid involves the transport of iodine from the blood to the thyroid follicle. Iodine is transported from the follicle to the colloid. Which pump or channel is for transport of iodine from the follicle to the colloid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pendrin

The channel needed for the transport of iodine from the follicle to the colloid is Pendrin.

Steps in synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormone:

• Iodide uptake: The basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) actively takes up I-(iodide) from the circulation into the follicular cells. It is then transported into the colloid through a pendrin (chloride-iodide) transporter
• Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin (Tg), is a large glycoprotein rich in tyrosine residues. It is synthesized by follicular cells.
• Iodination of Tg: This is regulated by the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme. TPO has three functions:
• Oxidation: TPO oxidizes I- to I2 (iodine)  in the presence of H2O2
• Organification: TPO links tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin with iodine (I2) to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT)
• Coupling reactions: TPO combines iodinated tyrosine residues to make MIT + DIT = T3 (triiodothyronine), DIT + DIT = T4 (tetraiodothyronine)
• Storage: Thyroid hormones are bound to thyroglobulin and stored in the follicular lumen as colloids. The colloid has hormone reserves for 2-3 months
• Release: Iodinated thyroglobulin is taken up by the thyroid follicles via endocytosis and fuses with lysosomes. It is cleaved by lysosomal proteolytic enzymes into MIT, DIT, T3, and T4. T4 (80%) and T3 (20%) are released into the blood
• Peripheral T3 conversion: T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone.

Pendred syndrome: Pendrin is present in the thyroid gland and inner ear. The mutation causes goiter and sensorineural hearing loss.

Other options

Option A: Sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is responsible for transporting iodine from the bloodstream into the thyroid follicular cell, not into the colloid. It works by bringing in iodine along with sodium from the bloodstream into the follicle.

Option B: Calmodulin is structurally and functionally related to troponin. In place of troponin, smooth muscle cells contain a large amount of the regulatory protein calmodulin; it is different in the manner in which it initiates contraction. Calmodulin initiates contraction by activating the myosin light chain kinase.

Option C: Claudin is a transmembrane protein involved in the formation of tight junctions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident while driving a car. On examination, the affected lower limb appears shortened. A pelvic radiograph (shown below) demonstrates characteristic findings. In this condition, which nerve is most commonly injured?
questions.explanation: The pelvis radiograph shows a "posterior hip dislocation," where the femoral head is displaced behind the acetabulum. This injury classically occurs in "dashboard accidents" where the knee strikes the dashboard, driving the femur backward. The "sciatic nerve" (Option A) passes directly posterior to the hip joint and is the "most commonly injured nerve" in this condition, occurring in about 10–20% of cases. Sciatic nerve palsy can lead to foot drop and sensory loss in the lower leg. The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (Option B), inferior gluteal nerve (Option C), and superior gluteal nerve (Option D) are also located in the gluteal region but are much less frequently involved in clinical hip trauma. A posterior hip dislocation is an orthopedic emergency requiring urgent reduction to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head. A thorough neurological examination of the foot and leg is mandatory before and after reduction to assess for sciatic nerve integrity
questions.learning: The pelvis radiograph shows a "posterior hip dislocation," where the femoral head is displaced behind the acetabulum. This injury classically occurs in "dashboard accidents" where the knee strikes the dashboard, driving the femur backward.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man was admitted to the emergency ward with severe, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the left arm and profuse sweating. ECG showed ST-segment elevation in precordial leads. The person succumbed after 3 hours. During the autopsy, his heart was taken out and immersed in a solution. The normal area of the heart turned brick red whereas the infarcted portion turned white. Which of the following can be the likely component of the solution?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain imparts a brick red color to the intact non-infarcted myocardium whereas the infarcted portion appears white.

* Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

* This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved.

* Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding progesterone-only pills are correct? 1. They contain high-dose progesterone as there is no estrogen component. 2. They do not have “on and off” regimen. 3. They can be used with hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs. 4. The failure rate is 0.3 to 2 per hundred women-years of use. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 4

1. High-dose progesterone: Incorrect.

• Progestin-only pills (POPs) contain a low dose of progestin, not high-dose progesterone.
• They do not contain estrogen.

2. No “on and off” regimen: Correct.

• POPs are taken continuously every day, without the hormone-free interval used with combined oral contraceptives.

3. Can be used with hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs: Incorrect.

• Enzyme-inducing drugs can increase progestin metabolism and reduce contraceptive effectiveness.

4. Failure rate 0.3–2 per 100 woman-years: Correct.

• POPs are highly effective when taken correctly, with a low failure rate in typical exam-based figures.
questions.learning: High-dose progesterone: Incorrect. • Progestin-only pills (POPs) contain a low dose of progestin, not high-dose progesterone. • They do not contain estrogen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following does not form a boundary of the 'Triangle of Doom'? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inguinal ligament

The "Triangle of Doom" is an important anatomical danger zone encountered during laparoscopic hernia repair. This triangle contains critical structures, including the external iliac vessels that must be avoided during mesh fixation and dissection. This triangle is bounded by the vas deferens medially, the gonadal vessels laterally, and the peritoneal reflection forming the base. The inguinal ligament is not a boundary of this triangle in the laparoscopic perspective.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following acts as an inhibitor of Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) in the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyanide

Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) is the final enzyme of the electron transport chain (ETC) and is responsible for transferring electrons to oxygen, forming water.

Cyanide is a potent inhibitor of Complex IV. It binds to the ferric (Fe³⁺) iron of cytochrome a₃, blocking electron transfer to oxygen. This halts the entire ETC, leading to:

• Cessation of oxidative phosphorylation
• ↓ ATP production
• Cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acidosis
• Causes histotoxic hypoxia (oxygen is present but cannot be utilized)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Carbon dioxide: Not an ETC inhibitor
• Oligomycin: Inhibits ATP synthase (Complex V)
• Antimycin A: Inhibits Complex III
questions.learning: Cyanide Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) is the final enzyme of the electron transport chain (ETC) and is responsible for transferring electrons to oxygen, forming water.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with continuous discomfort in the right hypochondrium. Upon examination, an enlarged liver 8cm below the costal margins is noted. The image below displays his CT radiograph. Additionally, he reports a history of spending a significant amount of time around pet dogs. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Echinococcus granulosus

The given clinical scenario along with  CT scan of the liver showing a hydatid cyst seen as a hypodense lesion with internal septation, suggests a diagnosis of Echinococcus granulosus. It is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Hydatid cysts result from infection by the Echinococcus, and can result in cyst formation anywhere in the body.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

Investigation:

* CT examination reveals a fluid density cyst, with frequent peripheral focal areas of calcification, which usually indicates no active infection if completely circumferential.

* Septation and daughter cysts may be visualised. The water-lily sign indicates a cyst with a floating, undulating membrane, caused by a detached endocyst.

* May also show hyperdense internal septa representing a spoke wheel pattern within a cyst.

The life cycle of Echinococcus is depicted in the image below:
questions.learning: Echinococcus granulosus — The given clinical scenario along with CT scan of the liver showing a hydatid cyst seen as a hypodense lesion with internal septation, suggests a diagnosis of Echinococcus granulosus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presented with intussusception and was taken up for surgery. He was found to have multiple polyps. The resected section was sent for histopathology and the whole mount image of the specimen is given below. Identify the lesion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hamartomatous polyp

The given clinical feature of intussusception and multiple polyps and the histologic picture showing an arborizing pattern of connective tissue, smooth muscle, lamina propria, and glands are suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome, which is a type of hamartomatous polyp of the small intestine.

It is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract and melanosis of the mouth and the lips.

Clinical features:

• Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract
• Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, perianal skin, and digits
• Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum.
• Increased risk for extraintestinal malignant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles.

Management:

• Surgery is indicated in cases where there are bleeding, obstruction, intussusception, or adenomatous changes of the polyp.
• If surgery is done for these indications attempts should be made to remove as much as polyps as possible.
• Regular screening with endoscopic studies should be done due to the increased risk of malignancies.
• Screening of other malignancies like breast and cervix are also important.

Other options:

A) Tubulovillous adenoma:

These are a mixture of tubular and villous adenoma and consist of small, pedunculated polyps composed of rounded or tubular glands and larger, sessile polyps which are covered by slender villi. These adenomas are characterized microscopically by the presence of epithelial dysplasia. The hallmarks of epithelial dysplasia are nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation and stratification.

C) Adenocarcinoma:

Presents with occult bleeding, changes in bowel habits, or cramping and left lower quadrant discomfort. Morphologically, they present as polypoid, exophytic masses or annular lesions that produce ‘napkin-ring’ construction and luminal narrowing. Microscopically, these tumours consist of tall columnar cells with elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei and necrotic debris in the gland lumen.

D) Hyperplastic polyp:

Hyperplastic polyps, most commonly found in the left colon are smooth, nodular protrusions of the mucosa, often on the crests of mucosal folds. Histologically, they are composed of mature goblet and absorptive cells with a serrated surface architecture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 53-year-old patient with breast cancer and a history of heart failure is being evaluated for chemotherapy. Which of the following drugs should be avoided because it can worsen heart failure?
questions.explanation: In the treatment of breast cancer, the class of drugs known as anthracyclines, which includes Epirubicin and Doxorubicin, is notorious for causing dose-dependent, permanent cardiotoxicity . These drugs can induce cardiomyopathy and significantly exacerbate pre-existing heart failure (Option B). Therefore, in a patient with a documented history of cardiac failure, Epirubicin should be strictly avoided or used with extreme caution. Methotrexate (Option A), Cyclophosphamide (Option C), and Cisplatin (Option D) have other systemic toxicities (such as renal or pulmonary) but are not classically associated with the direct, profound cardiotoxicity seen with anthracyclines. Modern oncology protocols for cardiac patients often utilize "anthracycline-free" regimens to ensure patient safety. Regular monitoring of the ejection fraction via echocardiography is mandatory for any patient receiving epirubicin. Therefore, Epirubicin is the definitive pharmacological answer for the drug to avoid in this specific clinical scenario
questions.learning: In the treatment of breast cancer, the class of drugs known as anthracyclines, which includes Epirubicin and Doxorubicin, is notorious for causing dose-dependent, permanent cardiotoxicity .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy presents with a history of injury to the eye caused while climbing a tree 5 days ago, resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for 2 days. Slit-lamp examination reveals a lesion as shown below. Which among the following is a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Satellite lesion

The given clinical vignette and the image suggest that it is a fungal corneal ulcer. Satellite lesions are a feature of fungal ulcers.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms :

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.

Other options :

Option A: Reverse hypopyon is the collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. This can lead to complications such as glaucoma.

Option B: Dendritic ulcer is seen in epithelial keratitis caused by herpes simplex virus. An image of a dendritic ulcer with fluorescein dye is as shown below

Option C: Ring abscess is seen in helminthic keratitis, especially by acanthamoeba. There is gradual enlargement and coalescence of infiltrates which forms an abcess.

Relatively more pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Recurrences are characteristic.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is routinely administered preoperatively in patients with pheochromocytoma to control blood pressure and prevent hypertensive crises?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that causes severe paroxysmal hypertension. The gold-standard medication for preoperative management is Phenoxybenzamine. It is an irreversible, long-acting non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker that prevents the surge of blood pressure during tumor handling by binding to and receptors. Captopril (Option A, ACE inhibitor) and Nifedipine (Option C, CCB) can be used as adjuncts but are not the primary agents. Crucially, Propranolol (Option B, beta-blocker) must never be given alone before alpha-blockade is established. Blocking -mediated vasodilation while leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed can lead to a catastrophic, life-threatening hypertensive crisis. The standard "alpha-first" rule requires alpha-blockade for at least 10–14 days pre-surgery to allow for volume expansion. Beta-blockers are only added once alpha-blockade is effective, specifically to manage catecholamine-induced tachycardia. Proper preoperative preparation is essential for a safe surgical outcome
questions.learning: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that causes severe paroxysmal hypertension. The gold-standard medication for preoperative management is Phenoxybenzamine.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amnion

The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation.

The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell.

Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects.

Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.
questions.learning: Amnion — The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion. Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with bitemporal hemianopia, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, and features suggestive of acromegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a complex endocrine profile: amenorrhea and lactation (indicating excess prolactin) combined with acromegaly-like features (indicating excess growth hormone). This dual secretion is characteristic of a mammosomatotroph adenoma (Option C). The presence of bitemporal hemianopia confirms a large pituitary tumor (macroadenoma) compressing the optic chiasma. Corticotroph adenomas (Option A) cause Cushing's disease. Gonadotroph adenomas (Option B) are usually clinically non-functioning. Gliomas (Option D) are tumors of the brain parenchyma rather than the pituitary gland and would not typically cause this specific hormonal triad. Mammosomatotroph cells are a single cell type that can produce both GH and prolactin. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring serum GH, IGF-1, and prolactin, along with an MRI of the sella turcica. Therefore, the combined hormonal symptoms and the visual field defect identify the specific pituitary tumor subtype
questions.learning: The patient presents with a complex endocrine profile: amenorrhea and lactation (indicating excess prolactin) combined with acromegaly-like features (indicating excess growth hormone).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During screening for severe acute malnutrition, a 14-month-old child has a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of 11.5 cm. What is the nutritional classification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Severe acute malnutrition

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a simple, reliable screening tool used to assess acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months.

According to WHO criteria:

• MUAC <11.5 cm → Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM)
• MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm → Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM)
• MUAC ≥12.5 cm → Normal nutritional status

A MUAC of 11.5 cm is classified as Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in standard examination questions.

Why not the other options?

• A. Moderate acute malnutrition: MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm (many exam references use >11.5 to <12.5 cm).
• C. Normal nutritional status: MUAC ≥12.5 cm.
• D. Severe chronic malnutrition: Chronic malnutrition (stunting) is assessed using height-for-age Z-score, not MUAC.
questions.learning: Severe acute malnutrition Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a simple, reliable screening tool used to assess acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The standardized age mortality ratio is an indicator for which of the following?
options: Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution
Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard sex distribution
Removal of bias due to different age group population in different countries
To eliminate age structure of different countries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution

The age standardized mortality ratio (SMR) is an indicator of the death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution. It is obtained by indirect standardization and cannot be used to compare multiple groups with different age structures.

Standardized death rate (SDR) obtained by direct standardization enables comparisons of mortality rates between populations with different age compositions by eliminating the confounding effect caused by variations in age structures (Options C and D). This adjustment process can also account for factors such as sex, race, and parity.

Standardization can be achieved through two methods: direct or indirect. In both cases, a standard population is selected as a reference, characterized by known numbers in each age and sex group.

The direct method of standardization requires age-specific death rates (ASDR) along with the corresponding subgroup sizes. By applying these rates to the standard population, the expected deaths across all age groups can be calculated assuming that both populations share the same age-specific death rates. Dividing the total expected deaths by the standard population yields the SDR.

The calculated standardized death rate in direct standardization can be compared with different population groups with different age group compositions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-month-old child presented with umbilical discharge. Abdomen examination was normal except for the below finding. The next step of management is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. USG Abdomen

The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct). The next best step is the USG abdomen to diagnose if the anomaly is cystic, fibrous or fistula and it's connections.

Omphalomesenteric duct abnormalities: Vitello intestinal duct or omphalomesenteric duct is the connection between the yolk sac and the midgut during embryonic life, which eventually gets obliterated. The persistence of the vitellointestinal duct leads to various abnormalities depending on which part of the duct remains patent.

• Persistence of the proximal intestinal end of the duct leads to Meckel’s diverticula.
• Persistence of the distal end near the umbilicus leads to the umbilical polyp or sinus.
• Persistence of the distal end with mucus retention leads to the cyst, which may be associated with the intestine or the umbilicus by a fibrous band.
• A fully patent vitellointestinal duct can lead to an enterocutaneous fistula.

Patent urachus occurs due to the failure of urachus to obliterate, resulting in a connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

Urachal cyst occurs when the urachus fails to obliterate but there is no connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

The given image below shows a urachal cyst (UC) attached to Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) on one side and urinary bladder (UB) on the other side with a patent tract- urachus (U).
questions.learning: USG Abdomen — The given clinical image is that of a congenital umbilical anomaly such as patent urachus, urachal cyst, and vitelline cyst (resulting from the persistence of omphalomesenteric duct).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents with recurrent frontal headaches, prompting evaluation of the paranasal sinuses. Which radiographic view is best suited for optimal visualization of the frontal sinuses to assess for sinusitis?
questions.explanation: To evaluate the paranasal sinuses via conventional radiography, specific views are used for different anatomical areas. The Caldwell view (posteroanterior with a 15-degree downward tilt) is the most effective and standard view for detailed visualization of the frontal sinuses (Option B). It also provides good views of the ethmoid sinuses. Waters view (Option C) is the gold standard specifically for the maxillary sinuses. The lateral view (Option A) is useful for the sphenoid sinus and seeing the depth of the frontal sinus but provides poor overall detail compared to the frontal projections. The Submentovertex view (Option D) is primarily used for the skull base and zygomatic arches. Therefore, because the patient’s clinical concern is frontal sinusitis, the Caldwell view is the definitive radiological choice to clear that specific area. It allows the sinuses to be projected above the petrous ridges
