questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following stain can be used for laryngeal mass seen during laryngoscopic examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Supra vital

Laryngoscopic image shows growth over the vocal cords; supravital stain is used to detect laryngeal mass seen during laryngoscopic examination.

In the larynx, it is difficult to identify carcinoma in situ, early infiltrating carcinoma, and the exact margins of an established carcinoma. However, it has been found that the use of toluidine blue as a supravital stain during direct laryngoscopy is a reliable adjunct to the early and precise diagnosis of carcinoma of the larynx.

Also, toluidine blue staining is useful in improving the rate of negative resection margins of early glottic cancer (T1a–T2) treated by TLM (transoral oral microsurgery). This technique is called chromoendoscopy, where the interpretation is based on the colour: a dark blue (royal or navy) stain is considered positive, light blue staining is doubtful, and when no color is observed, it is interpreted as a negative stain, as shown below
questions.learning: Supra vital Laryngoscopic image shows growth over the vocal cords; supravital stain is used to detect laryngeal mass seen during laryngoscopic examination.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text:
Which of the following tests are not commonly used in osteoporosis:

1. DEXA
2. Bone scan
3. Quantitative CT
4. Chemical analysis
5. X-ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 & 3

Among the given options, bone scan and quantitative CT are not commonly used in the diagnosis of osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

DEXA, chemical tests and X-ray are commonly used in the diagnosis of osteoporosis. While quantitative CT also helps to measure bone mass density at the spine and hip, it is rarely used clinically because the radiation exposure and cost are both much higher than with DXA. A bone scan uses a radioactive tracer injected into the bloodstream to detect altered metabolic activity in the bone with the aid of a gamma camera. It is not used in the diagnosis of osteoporosis.

DEXA - dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. T-score less than or equal to 2.5 in the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip indicates osteoporosis.

Chemical tests like serum calcium, phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase levels are usually normal in primary osteoporosis and help to rule out other conditions before establishing a diagnosis of osteoporosis.

X-ray features of osteoporosis:

• Loss of vertical height of a vertebra occurs due to collapse
• Cod fish appearance characterized by the disc bulging into the adjacent vertebral bodies, resulting in a biconvex shape
• Ground glass appearance of the bones
questions.learning: 2 & 3 Among the given options, bone scan and quantitative CT are not commonly used in the diagnosis of osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a common metabolic bone disease characterised by a diffuse reduction in bone density due to a decrease in bone mass.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old patient with obstructive jaundice has a distended gall bladder and a dilated common bile duct and intrahepatic biliary radicles on ultrasound. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed the same findings with no additional findings. Which of the following will be most useful to localize the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Magnetic resonance imaging

The given clinical scenario with USG and CECT showing a distended gall bladder, dilated common bile duct, and intrahepatic biliary radicles raises suspicion of common bile duct stones (CBD stones). Among the given options, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI/MRCP) will be next most useful modality to localize the cause and level of obstruction.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) uses T2-weighted MRI sequences and it is highly sensitive and specific in identifying CBD stones. MRCP provides visualization of dilated bile ducts and often enables accurate assessment of the level of occlusion in the biliary tree. It is a non-invasive test and is preferred by many surgeons to assess the need for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). ERCP is also highly effective at diagnosing CBD stones. However, due to the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality, rather it is now used only as a therapeutic modality such as when stone extraction or sphincterotomy is planned (option D).

Ultrasonography (USG) can detect gallstones and assess the size of the common bile duct. If a patient with gallstones, jaundice, and biliary pain shows a dilated common bile duct (>8 mm in diameter) on USG, it strongly suggests the presence of CBD stones. CT scan is also a sensitive diagnostic tool for CBD stones. USG and CT will generally be the first line modalities due to their easier availability, and lower cost and time requirements.

Other options:

Option B- Endoscopic ultrasound is used for detecting CBD stones. It is considered as good as ERCP but it is invasive and requires expertise in endoscopic procedure and hence it is not done routinely.

Option C- Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) is rarely performed in patients with CBD stones. In patients where endoscopic or surgical procedures are contraindicated, it may be used for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
questions.learning: Magnetic resonance imaging — The given clinical scenario with USG and CECT showing a distended gall bladder, dilated common bile duct, and intrahepatic biliary radicles raises suspicion of common bile duct stones (CBD stones).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the correct statement regarding immune surveillance.
options: Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers
Mutation of tumor supressor genes decreases antigen toxicity
PD1/ PDL1 activation leading to tumor supression
Binding of CD28 leads to immune tolerance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers

Anti-CTLA-4 antibody ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) plays an important inhibitory role in the control of T-cell activation.

Ipilimumab is a fully-humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4).

It has been postulated that anti-CTLA-4 antibodies act by blocking inhibitory signals from effector T-cells, allowing costimulatory signaling and generation of antitumor T-cell responses. In vitro studies demonstrated also that the antitumor activity of CTLA-4 blockade is mediated by Fc gamma receptor-expressing macrophage and hypothesized a possible role of regulatory T-cell depletion in the tumor microenvironment.

Option B - Mutation of tumor supressor genes is associated with increased risk of cancer. Antigen toxicity is when the immune response to an antigen is excessive or misdirected, causing damage to tissues or organs.

Option C - PD1/PDL1 is an immune checkpoint whose activation inhibits T-cell function and helps with immune tolerance. Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction using immune checkpoint inhibitors reactivates T cells and enhances immune responses against tumors.

Option D - CD28 is primarily involved in providing the second signal required for T cell activation. The first signal comes from the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Without CD28-mediated costimulation, T cells that only receive the TCR signal (without the second signal) can become anergic.
questions.learning: Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers Anti-CTLA-4 antibody ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which nerve injury is most commonly responsible for the deformity seen in a patient with leprosy?
questions.explanation: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease that has a predilection for the peripheral nerves. The ulnar nerve is the most common nerve affected in the upper limb in leprosy patients (Option A) . Damage to the ulnar nerve at the elbow or wrist leads to the classic "claw hand" deformity, characterized by hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints of the ring and little fingers. Median nerve injury (Option C) leads to "ape thumb" deformity and is the second most common upper-limb nerve affected. Radial nerve injury (Option B) causing wrist drop is much less frequent. The posterior interosseous nerve (Option D) is a branch of the radial nerve. Because the ulnar nerve is uniquely susceptible to the thickening and inflammation caused by Mycobacterium leprae in its superficial course, it is the definitive answer for the primary neuro-orthopedic deformity in this population
questions.learning: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease that has a predilection for the peripheral nerves. The ulnar nerve is the most common nerve affected in the upper limb in leprosy patients (Option A) .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The USG given below is seen in:
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image depicts the classic "snowstorm" appearance (or "bunch of grapes" appearance), which is pathognomonic for a Hydatidiform Mole. This pattern is created by the hydropic degeneration of placental villi, appearing as multiple small cystic spaces filling an enlarged uterine cavity. A fetus is notably absent in a complete mole. Ectopic pregnancy (Option A) would show an empty uterus with an adnexal mass. Ovarian pregnancy (Option B) is a rare ectopic type. Anencephaly (Option C) is a fetal neural tube defect that would show a developing fetus lacking the cranial vault. Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD) also presents with vaginal bleeding and abnormally high serum beta-hCG levels. Management requires urgent suction evacuation and careful long-term follow-up to monitor for malignant transformation. Therefore, the distinctive "snowstorm" ultrasound visual is the defining characteristic of a molar pregnancy

Correct answer: C. District

• The principal unit of administration in India is the district under a Collector.
• Under districts are the sub-divisions, tahsils or talukas, municipalities or corporations, villages, panchayats, etc.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the arrow-marked structure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulmonary Trunk

The arrow marks the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk.

The image shows a cross section of a cadaver at the T5 vertebral level. This corresponds anteriorly to the level of the sternal angle, and is also the level of division between the superior and inferior mediastinum.

At this level, the other structures visible are:

• The origin and termination of the arch of aorta. The descending aorta can be identified to the left of the oesophagus. The arch of the aorta (Option D) would be visible at the T3-T4 cross sectional level.
• The superior vena cava (Option B), just lateral to the origin of the aorta, which can visually differentiated from the aorta based on the wall thickness. At this level, it penetrates the right atrium.
• The bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk.
• The left and right main bronchi. The carina (Option A) is not visible as the trachea bifurcates more proximally at the T4 level.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis from the given CT scan.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PUJ obstruction

The CT scan showing ballooning of the left renal pelvis with moderate hydronephrosis of the affected kidney indicating a likely diagnosis of ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJ)of the left side.

PUJ obstruction refers to a blockage or narrowing at the junction where the renal pelvis transitions into the ureter, leading to impaired drainage of urine from the kidney.

Indications for surgery in patients with UPJ obstruction include:

• On the diuretic renogram, UPJO with less than 40% in the split function of the afflicted kidney.
• Renal parenchymal atrophy in the presence of severe bilateral UPJO.
• Despite preventive medicines, recurring urinary tract infections.
• Obstructive UPJO that is symptomatic or linked with an abdominal mass

Hydronephrosis may be detected on antenatal ultrasound; it can, however, be transient or mild and resolves on its own. Re-evaluation should be done after birth and in cases presenting with symptoms of recurrent UTI, palpable flank mass or pain, urinary obstruction, and in cases of failure to thrive.

If the hydronephrosis is persistent, its severity is graded by the extent of the dilatation of the pelvicalyceal system and parenchymal thickness. It needs to be ascertained whether the other kidney is involved, the lower ureter is dilated, the bladder wall is thickened, and whether emptying of the bladder is incomplete. Based on these findings, a diagnosis can be made.

In cases of hydronephrosis, long-standing urine stasis and pressure may damage the kidneys.

The causes of UPJ obstruction are

• Intrinsic (due to an adynamic or stenotic segment of the proximal ureter) or
• Extrinsic (e.g. compression by accessory renal arteries). This needs to be corrected primarily.

The renal anatomy and function can be assessed using radioscintigraphy studies. The investigation of choice for UPJ obstruction is 99mTc-MercaptoAcetyl-triGlycine (MAG3) scan. Micturating cystourethrogram is the investigation of choice in vesicoureteric reflux. 99mTc-dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) scan is used for assessing renal scarring.

Treatment of intrinsic UPJ obstruction is done surgically if renal function is compromised or if there is bilateral involvement of the kidneys. In other cases, serial follow-up with ultrasonography is done to assess the spontaneous resolution of hydronephrosis.

Surgical options include pyeloplasty which entails the surgical division of the obstruction and the creation of a funnel-shaped anastomosis. Additionally, a temporary stent and a drain may be inserted. It is necessary to do further serial ultrasounds and MAG-3 imaging in order to ensure proper monitoring and evaluation. This procedure is now commonly being performed via laparoscopy and also with robotic assistance. Congenital PUJ obstruction is treated surgically by Anderson Hyen's pyeloplasty.

Below are CT scans of a left PUJ obstruction before(left) and after(right) surgery.

Other options:

Option B: A renal cyst would appear as a fluid-filled, well-demarcated structure within the kidney but does not involve the PUJ or cause obstruction.

Option C: A renal tumor would present as a solid, abnormal mass within the kidney, not typically involving the PUJ unless there is direct extension.

Option D: Multicystic kidney refers to the presence of multiple cysts within the kidney, often congenital, but is not specific to the PUJ and would not result in obstruction at the PUJ.
questions.learning: PUJ obstruction — The CT scan showing ballooning of the left renal pelvis with moderate hydronephrosis of the affected kidney indicating a likely diagnosis of ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJ)of the left side.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A man falls onto his shoulder with his head forced to the opposite side and subsequently develops the shown deformity. Which cervical nerve root values are most likely to be involved in this injury?
questions.explanation: A traumatic separation of the head and shoulder causes a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots. This results in Erb's Palsy, which presents with a characteristic "waiter's tip" posture where the arm is held limp by the side, internally rotated at the shoulder, and pronated at the forearm. C6 and C7 (Option B) involve the middle trunk and do not produce this specific classic posture. C7 and C8 (Option C) affect lower plexus functions like wrist and finger movement rather than the shoulder. C8 and T1 (Option D) involve the lower trunk, typically injured by upward arm traction, resulting in Klumpke's palsy, which presents with intrinsic hand muscle weakness and sometimes Horner's syndrome. Because the mechanism involves downward shoulder traction and affects the upper limb's proximal segments, C5 and C6 are the damaged roots
questions.learning: A traumatic separation of the head and shoulder causes a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What will be the level of the uterus on the postpartum day 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Two finger breadths below umbilicus

On the second day post-delivery, the level of the uterus lies at two finger breadths below the umbilicus.

24 hours post delivery is equal to Day 0 when uterus is just below the umbilicus.

Day 1 - 1 finger breadth below umbilicus

The rate of involution of the uterus can be clinically assessed by noting the fundal height of the uterus in relation to the symphysis pubis.

Involution of the uterus occurs due to a decrease in the size of muscle fibers. Following delivery, the fundus lies about 5 1/2 inches above the symphysis pubis. During the first 24 hours, the level remains constant, after which there is a steady decrease in height by half an inch in 24 hours, which approximately equals two finger breadth below the umbilicus on second-day post delivery. By the end of 2nd week, the uterus becomes a pelvic organ. The rate of involution slows down after this until 6 weeks. The uterus almost becomes normal in size by 6 weeks.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following substances enhances the absorption of iron from the diet?
questions.explanation: Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and is strongly influenced by the oxidation state of iron. Dietary non-heme iron is predominantly present in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which is poorly absorbed. For absorption to occur, ferric iron must be reduced to the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, which can then be transported across the intestinal mucosa via Divalent Metal Transporter-1 (DMT1). Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) plays a crucial role in this process. It acts as a powerful reducing agent, converting Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, thereby enhancing iron solubility and absorption. This is why vitamin C markedly increases the bioavailability of non-heme iron. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Calcium (Option A): Inhibits iron absorption when taken simultaneously in large amounts 2. Vitamin D (Option C): Regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism, not iron absorption 3. Vitamin K (Option D): Required for synthesis of clotting factors and bone health
questions.learning: Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and is strongly influenced by the oxidation state of iron. Dietary non-heme iron is predominantly present in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which is poorly absorbed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with a yellow- green, foul-smelling vaginal discharge associated with dysuria and dyspareunia, without itching. On speculum examination, the vulva and vaginal walls are inflamed. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The presence of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling, often frothy discharge accompanied by inflammation of the vaginal walls and dyspareunia (painful intercourse) is highly characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis. A specific sign often seen on speculum examination is the "strawberry cervix". Candida albicans (Option B) typically presents with a white, curdy (cottage cheese-like) discharge and intense itching, which is absent here. Gardnerella vaginalis (Option C) causes bacterial vaginosis, characterized by a thin, gray-white discharge with a "fishy" odor, but generally lacks significant vaginal inflammation or dyspareunia. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Option D) primarily causes cervicitis but can overlap; however, the classic description of the discharge favors Trichomoniasis. Treatment involves metronidazole for both the patient and their partner to prevent recurrence. Thus, Trichomonas is the most likely causative agent
questions.learning: The presence of a yellowish-green, foul-smelling, often frothy discharge accompanied by inflammation of the vaginal walls and dyspareunia (painful intercourse) is highly characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with weakness of the lower half of the face on the right side, while forehead wrinkling is preserved. The lesion is most likely located in which of the following?
options: Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve
Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve

An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face with preservation of forehead movements. This occurs because the upper facial muscles (forehead) receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation, whereas the lower facial muscles receive only contralateral corticobulbar innervation. Therefore, a unilateral UMN lesion affects only the contralateral lower face.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lower motor neuron of the facial nerve: Produces ipsilateral paralysis of the entire half of the face, including inability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile (e.g., Bell’s palsy).
• C. Trigeminal nerve (CN V): Supplies the muscles of mastication and facial sensation; it does not cause facial expression weakness.
• D. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII): Supplies the tongue muscles; injury causes tongue deviation toward the affected side, not facial weakness.
questions.learning: Upper motor neuron of the facial nerve — An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face with preservation of forehead movements.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man working in an iron factory presents with progressively worsening vision and changes in color perception. Ophthalmologic examination reveals iron deposits in the eyes. What is the most likely ocular condition in this patient?
questions.explanation: Siderosis bulbi is a vision-threatening condition caused by the chronic retention of an intraocular iron-containing foreign body. The patient's employment in an iron factory provides a significant clinical clue for accidental trauma. As the iron oxidizes, it releases toxic ions that deposit throughout the ocular tissues, including the iris (causing heterochromia), lens (causing cataract), and most importantly, the retina. Retinal toxicity leads to progressive vision loss, night blindness, and altered color perception. Hemochromatosis (Option B) is a systemic iron-overload disorder that rarely causes primary ocular iron deposits. Retinitis pigmentosa (Option C) is a genetic dystrophy that presents with similar symptoms but lacks the history of industrial exposure and specific iron deposits. Age-related macular degeneration (Option D) causes gradual central vision loss in elderly patients without iron involvement. Management involves the urgent surgical removal of the metallic foreign body. Even with removal, the electroretinogram (ERG) may show permanent damage if the condition was long-standing
questions.learning: Siderosis bulbi is a vision-threatening condition caused by the chronic retention of an intraocular iron-containing foreign body. The patient's employment in an iron factory provides a significant clinical clue for accidental trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During resection of the submandibular gland along with its duct, which of the following structure lying below the duct is most likely to be injured during the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglossal nerve

During submandibular gland resection with removal of the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), the nerve most at risk below the duct is the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

During submandibular gland surgery, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) runs below and deep to the submandibular duct (on the hyoglossus muscle) and is at risk of injury during deep dissection. The lingual nerve has a characteristic lateral-below-medial (LBM) relationship with the duct and is also at risk. Injury to the hypoglossal nerve results in ipsilateral tongue paralysis with deviation toward the side of the lesion.
questions.learning: Hypoglossal nerve During submandibular gland resection with removal of the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), the nerve most at risk below the duct is the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intern placed an intercostal drainage tube in a patient. Which of the following steps is incorrect?
options: Identified 5th intercostal space anterior to mid axillary line to place the tube
Inserted tube along the lower border of upper rib
Directed tube posteriorly to prevent injury
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inserted tube along the lower border of upper rib

An intercostal tube (ICD) is placed along the upper border of the lower rib at the 5th intercostal space (ICS) to prevent damage to the neurovascular bundle. Hence, option B is incorrect.

Chest tube insertion (thoracostomy) is indicated in pneumothorax, hemothorax, chylothorax, and pleural effusion in order to drain air/fluid from the pleural space.

The triangle of safety, usually in the 5th intercostal space, is the safest site for chest tube insertion, it is bound by:

1. anterior to the midaxillary line
2. above the horizontal line marked by the level of the nipple
3. below and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle

Contraindications include pulmonary adhesions, pulmonary trauma, coagulopathy, and diaphragmatic hernia.

Complications of this procedure:

1. Infection at the site of insertion
2. Unintentional injury to the lung - hemothorax
3. Intercostal nerve/ vessel injury
4. Subcutaneous hematoma/ emphysema
questions.learning: Inserted tube along the lower border of upper rib — An intercostal tube (ICD) is placed along the upper border of the lower rib at the 5th intercostal space (ICS) to prevent damage to the neurovascular bundle.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which cells are responsible for graft rejection?
questions.explanation: The immunological rejection of an organ or tissue transplant is a complex process primarily driven by the adaptive immune system. T cells (both CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic cells) are the central mediators of graft rejection. They recognize foreign HLA (MHC) antigens on the donor tissue, leading to direct cell-mediated cytotoxicity and the release of cytokines that recruit inflammatory cells. Macrophages (Option A) act as effector cells that cause tissue damage but are recruited and activated by T cells rather than initiating the specific recognition. B cells (Option C) and plasma cells (Option D) are involved in chronic and hyperacute rejection through the production of donor-specific antibodies, but the cellular immune response led by T cells is the primary mechanism in most acute rejections. Therefore, because T cells are the primary orchestrators of the recognition and destruction of non-self grafts, they are the correct answer
questions.learning: The immunological rejection of an organ or tissue transplant is a complex process primarily driven by the adaptive immune system. T cells (both CD4+ helper and CD8+ cytotoxic cells) are the central mediators of graft rejection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following gastrointestinal secretions contain bicarbonate? 1. Stomach 2. Saliva 3. Duodenal 4. Ileal Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 4

All four secretions can contain bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻):

| GI secretion | Key point

| ------------ | ---------

| 1. Stomach | Surface mucous cells secrete HCO₃⁻, forming the gastric mucosal bicarbonate barrier

| 2. Saliva | Contains HCO₃⁻, important for buffering

| 3. Duodenal | Brunner glands and pancreatic/biliary secretions provide abundant HCO₃⁻ to neutralize gastric acid

| 4. Ileal | Intestinal epithelial secretion contains HCO₃⁻; Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange contributes to intestinal bicarbonate handling

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient is evaluated for meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals lymphocytic predominance, low glucose levels, and elevated protein concentration. What is the most likely etiological agent?
questions.explanation: Analyzing CSF parameters is vital for identifying the type of meningitis. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) characteristically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis (lymphocytosis), significantly decreased glucose, and marked elevation of protein. This profile reflects a chronic granulomatous inflammatory process. Acute bacterial pathogens like S. pneumoniae (Option A), H. influenzae (Option B), and N. meningitidis (Option C) would typically show a neutrophilic predominance (not lymphocytosis) alongside low glucose and high protein. Viral meningitis would show lymphocytosis but with normal glucose levels. TBM is a medical emergency with an insidious onset; it often results in thick basal exudates and cranial nerve palsies. Definitive diagnosis involves AFB staining, GeneXpert, or liquid culture (MGIT). Treatment requires a prolonged course of anti-tubercular therapy combined with corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and prevent neurological sequelae
questions.learning: Analyzing CSF parameters is vital for identifying the type of meningitis. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) characteristically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis (lymphocytosis), significantly decreased glucose, and marked elevation of protein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presents for a routine antenatal checkup at 18 weeks of gestation. On abdominal examination, the uterine size was found to correspond to 16 weeks of gestation. On USG, oligohydramnios was found. Which of the following is a likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renal agenesis

Among the given options, renal agenesis is the likely cause. It causes oligohydramnios in the early second trimester.

Fetal urine production starts between 8-11 weeks of gestation but becomes a major component of amniotic fluid only in the second trimester. Thus, oligohydramnios is not seen until after 18 weeks of gestation in fetuses with lethal renal abnormalities.

Oligohydramnios occurs when the amniotic fluid index (AFI) is <5 cm or the single deepest vertical pocket is <2 cm. AFI between 5-8 cm is known as borderline oligohydramnios.

Diagnosis of oligohydramnios:

•  Uterine size is much smaller than the period of amenorrhea
•  Less fetal movements
•  The uterus is ‘full of fetus’ due to scanty liquor
•  Malpresentation (breech) is common
•  Evidence of intrauterine growth retardation of the fetus is seen
•  Sonographic diagnosis is made when the largest liquor pool is less than 2 cm

Other options:

Fetal anemia, Bartter syndrome and Liddle syndrome usually lead to polyhydramnios and not oligohydramnios.
questions.learning: Renal agenesis Among the given options, renal agenesis is the likely cause. It causes oligohydramnios in the early second trimester.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which is not given in Wilson's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Calcium citrate

Calcium citrate is not used in the treatment of Wilson's disease.

The drugs used in the management of Wilson's disease are:

Chelating agents: These drugs bind to copper to form complexes that get excreted in the urine. D-penicillamine and trientine are first-line drugs in symptomatic patients with hepatic diseases.

• D-penicillamine: It is the recommended drug due to its availability and cost-effectiveness as compared to trientine. Since it is an antagonist to pyridoxine, supplementation of pyridoxine is required. It can precipitate various adverse effects including aplastic anemia, myasthenia gravis, and membranous nephropathy. It can also worsen neurological symptoms
• Trientine: It is administered in those who cannot tolerate D-penicillamine
• Tetrathiomolybdate: It has been identified to be effective in patients with neuropsychiatric manifestation

Elemental zinc:

• Zinc blocks the intestinal absorption of copper by inducing metallothionein (endogenous chelator in enterocytes)
• It is commonly used as a maintenance therapy along with chelating agents. It can also be used as first-line therapy in pregnancy
questions.learning: Calcium citrate Calcium citrate is not used in the treatment of Wilson's disease. The drugs used in the management of Wilson's disease are: Chelating agents: These drugs bind to copper to form complexes that get excreted in the urine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The given image shows what grade of placenta previa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. III

The given image shows grade III placenta previa.

Placenta previa refers to the placenta implanted (partially/completely) over the lower uterine segment (over or adjacent to the internal os). Grades of placenta previa are:

•  Type—I (Low-lying): The major part of the placenta is attached to the upper segment and only the
lower margin encroaches onto the lower segment but not up to the os.
• Type—II (Marginal): The placenta reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it.
• Type—III (Incomplete or partial central): The placenta covers the internal os partially (covers the
internal os when closed but does not entirely do so when fully dilated).
• Type—IV (Central or total): The placenta completely covers the internal os even after it is fully dilated.

They typically present with sudden onset, painless vaginal bleeding. On vulval inspection, bright red blood is seen oozing from the cervical opening. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is used to confirm the diagnosis and position of the placenta.

Management is dependent on the presentation of the patient. If there is a need for fetal maturity, expectant management (advocated by McAfee and Johnson) is carried out without increasing undue maternal stress. Definitive management by an elective cesarean section.
questions.learning: III — The given image shows grade III placenta previa. Placenta previa refers to the placenta implanted (partially/completely) over the lower uterine segment (over or adjacent to the internal os).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought with a lesion involving the right eye. Histopathological examination shows Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. Based on this finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic for Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. These rosettes consist of a ring of columnar tumor cells surrounding a central lumen, representing an attempt at retinal differentiation. Clinically, retinoblastoma characteristically presents in a young child (most often before age 5) with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex or "cat's eye" reflex) and occasionally strabismus. Optic nerve glioma (Option B) is a tumor of the nerve itself, not the retina. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C) is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but does not originate within the eye. Ocular melanoma (Option D) is the most common primary eye cancer in adults, not children. Early diagnosis of retinoblastoma is critical to save both the life and the vision of the child. Treatment modalities include chemotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and enucleation in advanced cases
questions.learning: The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic for Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most probable diagnosis of given image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a heliotrope rash—a characteristic violaceous/purple discoloration of the upper eyelids, often accompanied by periorbital edema. This rash is a pathognomonic skin finding for Dermatomyositis, an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy. Other classic skin features include Gottron papules over the knuckles and a "shawl sign" on the back. Polymyositis (Option A) involves similar muscle weakness but lacks the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis. Inclusion body myositis (Option C) typically affects older males and involves distal muscle weakness without a primary rash. Discoid lupus erythematosus (Option D) presents with well-defined, scarred plaques, usually in different facial locations than the eyelids. Dermatomyositis requires a comprehensive workup because it is associated with an increased risk of internal malignancies, particularly in older adults. Management involves high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents. The heliotrope rash is the key clinical anchor for differentiating these inflammatory muscle diseases
questions.learning: The image depicts a heliotrope rash—a characteristic violaceous/purple discoloration of the upper eyelids, often accompanied by periorbital edema. This rash is a pathognomonic skin finding for Dermatomyositis, an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A farmer was sleeping in the field, and he felt a sting on his leg. He saw something moving away quickly. He then got drowsy and was taken to the hospital. He developed pain around the site and continued to bleed profusely from the wound site. The wound became red with blisters. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viper

Based on the given clinical findings, the most likely cause is a bite of viper snake, resulting in a haemotoxic envenomation.

The Russell's viper has a flat and triangular head with a V-shaped mark, white in color, with the angle of the V pointing forwards. Along the back, it has three rows of diamond-shaped spots. Other points of identification include broad plates on its belly, the small scales on the head, and a shield beneath the tail divided into two rows. It is commonly found throughout India.

Patients with Russell's viper bite usually present with severe pain, and redness around the bite site. Swelling usually develops followed by blisters in and around the wound site. Persistent bleeding from the bite site is a constant feature. Patients may develop hemorrhagic syndrome due to bleeding from various sites like gums, nose, rectum, etc. In severe cases, shock may develop. Bleeding and clotting time are usually prolonged. Death usually occurs due to shock or hemorrhage.

Other options:

Option B: Cobra venom usually produces neurotoxic effects with minimal local effects. Neurological manifestations of cobra venom include ptosis, paralysis of the face, palate, jaws, tongue, neck muscles, muscles of deglutition, and respiratory muscles.

Option C: Wasp stings cause immediate pain, a wheal and flare reaction, and local edema and swelling that subside in a few hours. Multiple stings can lead to vomiting, diarrhea, generalized edema, dyspnea, hypotension, and collapse.

Option D: Scorpion sting usually presents with localized redness and burning pain which is unable to localize due to its radiation along the dermatomes involved, localized swelling, and punctate hemorrhagic spots. Other features include headache, profuse perspiration, chest discomfort, paraesthesias, hypersalivation, cold extremities, and sometimes, priapism. Hypertension usually develops early, while pulmonary edema and myocarditis may develop later.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about laryngeal cancer stage T1bNOMO?
options: Both vocal cords involved and fixed
Both vocal cords involved, and No metastasis
One vocal cord involved and metastasis
One vocal cord involved, and mobile
questions.explanation: According to the TNM staging for glottic laryngeal cancer: T1a : Tumor limited to one vocal cord; normal mobility. T1b : Tumor involves both vocal cords; normal mobility. T2 : Tumor extends to supra- or subglottis, or impaired cord mobility. N0: No regional lymph node metastasis. M0: No distant metastasis. Therefore, the statement "Both vocal cords involved, and No metastasis" accurately describes the T1bN0M0 stage. Option A is incorrect as vocal cord "fixation" would make it a T3 tumor. Option C is incorrect due to the "M0" status. Option D describes a T1a tumor. Stage T1b tumors are early-stage cancers with an excellent prognosis. They are typically treated with either radiotherapy or endoscopic CO2 laser excision. Preserving the quality of the voice while ensuring oncological cure is the primary goal of management at this stage. Accurate knowledge of these staging nuances is critical for planning the appropriate surgical or radiation therapy
